docs.title: PIDL
docs.text:
Protocol Interaction Description Language - A JSON-based DSL for describing protocol choreography that compiles to diagrams.

PIDL models protocols as directed interaction graphs between entities, enabling generation of sequence diagrams, data flow diagrams, and other visualizations. It's designed for protocols where the primary concern is "who talks to whom, in what order" rather than message schemas or transport details.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• JSON-based DSL for describing protocol flows
  • Multiple output formats: PlantUML, Mermaid, Graphviz DOT, D2, SVG
  • Animated SVG with CSS flow visualizations and moving dots
  • Network boundary diagrams for trust zone visualization
  • SVG templates: default, minimal, sketch, blueprint, dark, high-contrast
  • Accessibility: WCAG AA compliant high-contrast template
  • Phase boxes: Visual grouping of flows by phase with color-coded depth
  • Interactive SVG: Hover effects on participants, messages, and flow dots
  • Animation effects: Pulse and glow for error/warning/highlight presets
  • Built-in examples: OAuth 2.0, PKCE, OIDC, MCP, A2A
  • CLI tool for validation and diagram generation
  • Go library for programmatic use
  • Conditional flows with condition field for when clauses
  • Alternative paths with alternatives for error handling and branching
  • Annotations with typed notes (security, performance, deprecated, etc.)
  • Nested phases with parent hierarchy support
  • State model with entity states and state transitions
  • State diagrams via Mermaid stateDiagram-v2 output
  • Protocol composition with imports and inheritance
  • Protocol simulation with state tracking and execution traces
  • Protocol comparison (diff) for change detection
  • Interactive debugger for step-through protocol execution
  • Security analysis with attack surface detection rules

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "simple-request",
    "name": "Simple Request/Response"
  },
  "entities": [
    {"id": "client", "name": "Client", "type": "client"},
    {"id": "server", "name": "Server", "type": "server"}
  ],
  "flows": [
    {"from": "client", "to": "server", "action": "request", "mode": "request"},
    {"from": "server", "to": "client", "action": "response", "mode": "response"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: go install github.com/grokify/pidl/cmd/pidl@latest

docs.title: Generate Diagrams
docs.text:
# PlantUML
pidl generate -f plantuml protocol.json

# Mermaid
pidl generate -f mermaid protocol.json

# D2
pidl generate -f d2 protocol.json

# SVG sequence diagram
pidl generate -f svg protocol.json

# Animated SVG with flow dots
pidl generate -f svg-animated --theme=dark protocol.json

# SVG with template
pidl generate -f svg --template=high-contrast protocol.json

# Network boundary diagram
pidl generate -f svg-network protocol.json

# Mermaid state diagram
pidl generate -f mermaid-state protocol.json

# State diagram for specific entity
pidl generate -f mermaid-state --entity=client protocol.json

docs.title: Protocol Architecture
docs.text: PIDL models protocols as directed graphs where nodes are entities/components and edges are interactions/relationships.

docs.title: Entity Types
docs.text:
Entity types are classified as client-side (initiators) or server-side (responders):

Type Classification Description client Client Application or service initiating requests user Client Human actor browser Client User agent / web browser agent Client AI/LLM agent delegated_agent Client Agent receiving delegated tasks (A2A) authorization_server Server Issues tokens and handles authentication resource_server Server Hosts protected resources identity_provider Server Authenticates users and issues identity assertions service_provider Server Consumes identity assertions server Server Generic server tool_server Server Exposes tools via protocol (MCP) tool Other Individual tool capability other Other Custom entity type

docs.title: Protocol Roles
docs.text:
Entities can implement protocol-specific roles:

Protocol Description Common Roles oauth OAuth 2.0 / OIDC authorization_server, client, resource_server scim SCIM Provisioning client, service_provider spiffe SPIFFE Identity workload, spire_server, spire_agent aauth Agent Authentication person_server, access_server, client idjag ID-JAG Identity client, person_server, access_server authzen AuthZEN Authorization pep, pdp, pip, pap mcp Model Context Protocol client, server, tool a2a Agent-to-Agent client_agent, remote_agent

docs.title: Deployment Components
docs.text:
Components group entities into logical deployment units:

Component Type Description Example Products idp Identity Provider Okta, Entra ID, Auth0 agent_provider AI Agent Platform Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini person_server AAuth Person Server Identity verification service access_server AAuth Access Server Token issuance service pdp Policy Decision Point OPA, Cedar, Topaz gateway API Gateway Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway mcp_client MCP Client Claude Code, Cursor mcp_server MCP Server Custom tool servers resource_api Resource API Backend services spire SPIFFE Runtime SPIRE Server/Agent

docs.title: Edges
docs.text: PIDL supports two types of edges: protocol flows (sequential actions) and trust relationships (static trust).

docs.title: Protocol Flows (Sequential Actions)
docs.text:
Flows are ordered interactions between entities that define protocol choreography. They generate sequence diagrams.

Field Description from Source entity ID to Target entity ID action Action identifier mode Flow type: request, response, redirect, callback, event, tool_call, tool_result phase Optional phase grouping condition Optional conditional execution alternatives Optional alternative paths

docs.title: Diagram Outputs
docs.text:
PIDL generates multiple diagram types from the same protocol definition:

Diagram Type Format Source Data Description Sequence Diagram plantuml, mermaid, d2, svg, svg-animated Flows Shows ordered interactions between entities Data Flow Diagram dot, d2-flow Flows Shows data movement between entities Architecture Diagram d2-arch Entities, Flows Shows system architecture Network Diagram svg-network Entities, Trust Levels Shows network boundaries and trust zones State Diagram mermaid-state Entity States, Flows Shows entity state machines Component Diagram (planned) Components Shows logical deployment units Trust Diagram (planned) Trust Relations Shows trust relationships between entities

docs.title: Target Protocols
docs.text:
PIDL is designed for describing:

  • Authentication/Authorization: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML
  • Agent Protocols: MCP (Model Context Protocol), A2A (Agent-to-Agent)
  • API Flows: Multi-party API choreography

docs.title: PIDL Specification
docs.text: Protocol Interaction Description Language v1.0

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
PIDL (Protocol Interaction Description Language) is a JSON-based DSL for describing protocol choreography. It models protocols as directed interaction graphs between entities, enabling generation of sequence diagrams, data flow diagrams, and other visualizations.

PIDL is designed for protocols where the primary concern is "who talks to whom, in what order" rather than message schemas or transport details. Target protocols include OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, MCP (Model Context Protocol), and A2A (Agent-to-Agent).

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. Choreography-focused: Models interactions between systems, not API endpoints
  2. Transport-agnostic: No HTTP methods, URLs, or wire formats
  3. Diagram-first: Optimized for generating visual representations
  4. JSON-native: Simple parsing, strict validation, universal tooling

docs.title: Document Structure
docs.text:
A PIDL document is a JSON object. It describes either one flow (flows) or an ordered list of named scenarios (scenarios):

{
  "protocol": { ... },
  "entities": [ ... ],
  "phases": [ ... ],
  "flows": [ ... ],
  "scenarios": [ ... ]
}
Section Required Description protocol Yes Metadata about the protocol entities Yes Participants in the protocol, in display order phases No Logical grouping of flows flows One of flows or scenarios Interactions between entities, as a single flow scenarios One of flows or scenarios Named, ordered sequences of flows (see Scenarios) metadata No Tokens, networks, components and trust relations

docs.title: Protocol Metadata
docs.text:
The protocol object contains metadata about the protocol being described.

{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "oauth2-authorization-code",
    "name": "OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow",
    "version": "1.0",
    "description": "OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Grant as defined in RFC 6749",
    "category": "auth",
    "references": [
      {
        "name": "RFC 6749",
        "url": "https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749"
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Protocol Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description id string Yes Unique identifier (lowercase, alphanumeric, hyphens) name string Yes Human-readable name version string No Version of this protocol description description string No Brief description category enum No One of: auth, agent, messaging, provisioning, other references array No Links to specifications

docs.title: Reference Object
docs.text: Field Type Required Description name string Yes Reference name (e.g., "RFC 6749") url string Yes URL to the reference

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
Entities represent participants in the protocol: systems, services, actors, or trust domains.

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "client",
      "name": "Client Application",
      "type": "client",
      "description": "Application requesting access to protected resources"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Entity Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description id string Yes Unique identifier (lowercase, alphanumeric, underscores) name string Yes Human-readable display name type enum Yes Entity type classification description string No Role description

docs.title: Entity Types
docs.text: Type Description Typical Use client Application or service initiating requests OAuth clients, API consumers authorization_server Issues tokens and handles authentication OAuth/OIDC providers resource_server Hosts protected resources APIs, data services user Human actor End users, resource owners browser User agent Web browsers agent AI/LLM agent MCP agents, A2A agents tool_server Exposes tools via protocol MCP tool servers tool Individual tool MCP tools delegated_agent Agent receiving delegated tasks A2A secondary agents identity_provider Authenticates users SAML IdPs service_provider Relies on identity provider SAML SPs server Generic server General purpose other Custom entity type Extension point

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
Phases provide optional logical grouping of flows for readability and diagram organization. Phases support hierarchical nesting via the parent field.

{
  "phases": [
    {
      "id": "authorization",
      "name": "Authorization",
      "description": "User authentication and consent"
    },
    {
      "id": "mfa",
      "name": "Multi-Factor Authentication",
      "parent": "authorization",
      "description": "Optional MFA challenge"
    },
    {
      "id": "token_exchange",
      "name": "Token Exchange",
      "description": "Exchange code for tokens"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Phase Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description id string Yes Unique identifier name string Yes Human-readable name description string No Phase description parent string No Parent phase ID for nesting

docs.title: Phase Hierarchy
docs.text:
Phases can be nested to create hierarchical groupings:

  • A phase with no parent is a root phase
  • A phase with a parent must reference a valid phase ID
  • Circular references are not allowed
  • A phase cannot be its own parent

Phases are rendered as grouping constructs in diagrams:

  • PlantUML: Colored box containers
  • Mermaid: Colored rect blocks
  • D2: Nested groups

docs.title: Flows
docs.text:
Flows are the core semantic unit: directed interactions between entities.

{
  "flows": [
    {
      "from": "client",
      "to": "auth_server",
      "action": "token_request",
      "label": "POST /token",
      "mode": "request",
      "phase": "token_exchange",
      "description": "Exchange authorization code for access token",
      "condition": "code_valid",
      "note": "Code must be exchanged within 10 minutes",
      "annotations": [
        {"type": "security", "text": "Validate code verifier (PKCE)"}
      ],
      "alternatives": [
        {
          "condition": "code_invalid",
          "flows": [
            {"from": "auth_server", "to": "client", "action": "error", "mode": "response"}
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Flow Fields
docs.text:
Field Type Required Description from string Yes¹ Source entity ID to string Yes¹ Target entity ID action string Yes¹ Action identifier include string No ID of a fragment scenario to insert here (scenarios only; see Include Steps) label string No Display label (defaults to action) mode enum No Interaction mode (defaults to request) phase string No Phase ID this flow belongs to description string No Detailed description sequence integer No Deprecated. Display-only step number; never affects order (see Ordering) condition string No Conditional execution clause note string No Visible note displayed on diagram annotations array No Typed annotations for tooling alternatives array No Alternative flow paths verification object No Evidentiary provenance (tier/source/citation) example object No Illustrative request, response and decoded tokens (see Flow Examples)

¹ Not set on an include step, which has include instead.

docs.title: Flow Verification
docs.text:
Records the evidentiary provenance of a flow — used for incident attack-flows where every step should trace to a source (or be marked reproduced/inferred).

Field Type Required Description tier enum Yes reported | corroborated | reproduced | partially_reproduced source string No Originating source (e.g. "OpenAI technical report", "METR") citation string No URL or reference locating the source 
{
  "from": "agent", "to": "target", "action": "exfiltrate",
  "verification": {"tier": "corroborated", "source": "METR", "citation": "https://metr.org/..."}
}

The tier vocabulary matches the aisecurity-incidents deepdive.json.

docs.title: Flow Modes
docs.text: Mode Description Diagram Representation request Synchronous request Solid arrow -> response Synchronous response Dashed arrow --> redirect HTTP redirect Solid arrow with redirect annotation callback Callback/webhook Solid arrow with callback annotation interactive Human interaction Solid arrow (user involved) event Asynchronous event Dashed arrow tool_call Tool invocation (MCP) Solid arrow with tool annotation tool_result Tool result (MCP) Dashed arrow with result annotation

docs.title: Conditional Flows
docs.text:
The condition field specifies when a flow is executed. Conditions are rendered as opt blocks in sequence diagrams.

{
  "from": "client",
  "to": "server",
  "action": "refresh_token",
  "condition": "token_expired"
}

docs.title: Annotations
docs.text:
Annotations provide typed metadata for flows. They are rendered as notes in diagrams.

{
  "annotations": [
    {
      "type": "security",
      "text": "Validate PKCE code_verifier",
      "details": "Compare SHA256(code_verifier) with stored code_challenge"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Annotation Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description type enum Yes Annotation category text string Yes Annotation message details string No Additional context

docs.title: Annotation Types
docs.text: Type Description security Security considerations performance Performance implications deprecated Deprecated functionality info General information warning Warning conditions error Error conditions

docs.title: Alternative Paths
docs.text:
The alternatives field defines branching paths from a flow. They are rendered as alt/else blocks in sequence diagrams.

{
  "from": "client",
  "to": "server",
  "action": "authenticate",
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "condition": "invalid_credentials",
      "description": "Authentication failed",
      "flows": [
        {"from": "server", "to": "client", "action": "auth_error", "mode": "response"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "condition": "mfa_required",
      "description": "Multi-factor authentication needed",
      "flows": [
        {"from": "server", "to": "client", "action": "mfa_challenge", "mode": "response"},
        {"from": "client", "to": "server", "action": "mfa_response", "mode": "request"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Alternative Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description condition string Yes Condition that triggers this path flows array Yes Flows in this alternative path description string No Description of this alternative

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
A protocol often has several journeys through the same roles: AAuth has five access modes, OAuth has several grants. Instead of one file per journey, a document can hold an ordered list of named scenarios that share the same entities, phases and metadata.

{
  "protocol": {"id": "demo", "name": "Demo"},
  "entities": [
    {"id": "person", "name": "Person", "type": "user"},
    {"id": "agent", "name": "Agent", "type": "agent"},
    {"id": "ps", "name": "Person Server", "type": "authorization_server"}
  ],
  "scenarios": [
    {
      "id": "three-party",
      "name": "PS authorization",
      "flows": [
        {"from": "agent", "to": "ps", "action": "auth_token_request"},
        {"include": "consent"},
        {"from": "ps", "to": "agent", "action": "auth_token", "mode": "response"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "consent",
      "name": "User consent",
      "fragment": true,
      "flows": [
        {"from": "ps", "to": "person", "action": "consent_prompt"},
        {"from": "person", "to": "ps", "action": "approve", "mode": "response"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

A document has either flows or scenarios. A document with flows behaves as a single unnamed scenario, so existing files keep working.

docs.title: Scenario Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description id string Yes Unique identifier, matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*$ name string Yes Display name description string No Description of the scenario participants array No Entity IDs to show, in entities order. Defaults to the entities the scenario uses, including those of included fragments fragment boolean No Marks a reusable sub-flow that other scenarios include flows array Yes The scenario's steps, in order

docs.title: Include Steps and Fragments
docs.text:
A step {"include": "<scenario-id>"} inserts a fragment's flows at that point. The target must be a scenario with "fragment": true, and includes must not form a cycle. An include step may also set phase, condition, label, note, description and annotations; inlined flows inherit the include's phase and condition when they have none of their own.

Diagram formats draw an include step as a labeled box spanning the fragment's participants (PlantUML ref over, a shaded Mermaid rect, a D2 group, an SVG box), or inline the fragment's flows when expanded.

Fragments are listed after main scenarios wherever scenarios are numbered, so a deck or file listing shows the journeys first and the shared pieces after them.

docs.title: Working with One Scenario
docs.text: Most outputs describe one flow. Tools select a scenario and project it into a single-flow protocol: the scenario's flows, its participants (in entities order), the phases it uses, and the shared metadata. In the Go library this is Protocol.Scenario(id, ProjectOptions{Expand: ...}); on the command line it is --scenario <id>.

docs.title: Token Verification
docs.text:
Token definitions and flow security can say who checks what, so reviews and generated tables show where each guarantee is enforced:

Field On Description verified_by token definition Entity IDs that check the token claims token definition Claims checkers rely on, each with name, checked_by and description signed_by flow security Entity that signs the request, when it is not the sender issues flow security Token IDs the flow delivers verifies flow security Token IDs the receiver checks

issues and verifies let tools follow a token through a scenario: who it was delivered to, who presents it, and who signs the request that carries it.

docs.title: Flow Examples
docs.text:
A flow can carry an illustrative message for walkthrough viewers. Examples explain a protocol; they are not message schemas.

{
  "from": "agent", "to": "ps", "action": "auth_token_request",
  "example": {
    "source": "draft-11 §7.2.1",
    "kind": "draft",
    "request": {
      "method": "POST",
      "url": "https://ps.example/token",
      "headers": [
        {"name": "Content-Type", "value": "application/json"},
        {"name": "Signature-Key", "value": "sig=jwt;jwt=\"eyJ...\""}
      ],
      "body": {"resource_token": "eyJ...", "presented_token": "eyJ..."}
    },
    "tokens": [
      {"token": "resource_token", "label": "request body",
       "header": {"alg": "Ed25519", "typ": "aa-resource+jwt"},
       "payload": {"iss": "https://resource.example", "agent_jkt": "kPrK..."}}
    ],
    "note": "The PS checks agent_jkt against the key that signed this request."
  }
}
Field Required Description source Yes Citation, such as a specification section kind Yes draft: taken from the source, values aligned to the scenario; derived: written from the source's normative text request One of request, response, tokens method, url, ordered headers (name, value) and a JSON body response One of request, response, tokens status, ordered headers and a JSON body tokens One of request, response, tokens Decoded tokens: token (a token definition ID), label, header and payload note No What the reader should notice

Headers are a list so they keep their order. Include steps cannot carry examples.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Order in PIDL comes from one source: the position of an item in its JSON array. Every output generated from a document (diagrams, tables, outlines, file listings) uses the same order, so presentations, guides and diagrams built from one file agree.

  1. Roles follow the order of entities. Diagram columns, role tables and any other list of entities use this order.
  2. Scenarios follow the order of scenarios.
  3. Phases follow the order of phases.
  4. Messages follow the order of flows (top-level or within a scenario). An include step expands in place.
  5. Derived lists keep the order of the array they come from. A subset of entities (such as a scenario's participants or a token's checkers) is listed in entities order, never in the order written.
  6. Collections keyed by name are arrays of objects with an id. The one exception is metadata.networks, a map kept for compatibility, which tools never read in map iteration order:
  7. Network boundaries are ordered by metadata.network_layout.order first. Boundaries it does not list follow by style (external, dmz, trusted, cloud, default) and then by ID.
  8. An entity listed in more than one network belongs to the network whose ID sorts last.
  9. Entities inside each boundary follow entities order, like every other list of entities. To list them alphabetically, sort the entities array.

Numeric ordering fields are not used. The sequence field on a flow is deprecated: it is a display-only step number, and tools must not sort by it.

docs.title: Validation Rules
docs.text:
1. All entity IDs referenced in flows must be defined in entities
  2. All phase IDs referenced in flows must be defined in phases
  3. A protocol must have at least 2 entities
  4. A protocol must have at least 1 flow, or at least 1 scenario that is not a fragment; a document with scenarios has no top-level flows
  5. Entity, phase and scenario IDs must be unique within their respective arrays
  6. IDs must match pattern: ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$ (entities/phases) or ^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*$ (protocol/scenarios)
  7. A scenario must have a name and at least 1 flow
  8. A flow is either a message (from, to, action) or an include step, and include steps appear only in scenarios
  9. An include must name a fragment scenario, and includes must not form a cycle
  10. A scenario's participants must name known entities, once each, in entities order, and must cover every entity the scenario uses
  11. Token and entity references in verified_by, claims, signed_by, issues and verifies must resolve

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
The canonical JSON Schema is available at:

  • Repository: schema/pidl.schema.json
  • URL: https://github.com/grokify/pidl/schema/pidl.schema.json

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Minimal OAuth 2.0 token exchange:

{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "oauth2-token-exchange",
    "name": "OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange"
  },
  "entities": [
    {"id": "client", "name": "Client", "type": "client"},
    {"id": "auth", "name": "Auth Server", "type": "authorization_server"}
  ],
  "flows": [
    {"from": "client", "to": "auth", "action": "token_request", "mode": "request"},
    {"from": "auth", "to": "client", "action": "token_response", "mode": "response"}
  ]
}

docs.title: File Extension
docs.text: PIDL files use the .pidl.json extension by convention.

docs.title: Process Profile
docs.text: PIDL supports a process profile for describing data processing workflows in addition to the standard protocol profile. Process specs model step-by-step data transformations with explicit input/output ports, processing characteristics, and failure handling.

docs.title: Protocol Kind
docs.text:
The kind field in the protocol metadata distinguishes between protocol and process specifications:

{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "etl-pipeline",
    "name": "ETL Pipeline",
    "kind": "process"
  }
}
Kind Description protocol Standard protocol (default) - models interactions between systems process Process specification - models data processing workflows

docs.title: Step Types
docs.text:
In process specifications, entities represent processing steps. The step_type field classifies each step:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "extract",
      "name": "Data Extraction",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "deterministic"
    },
    {
      "id": "transform",
      "name": "LLM Transform",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "llm"
    }
  ]
}
Step Type Icon Description Characteristics deterministic ⚙️ Predictable processing Same input → same output llm 🧠 AI/ML processing Non-deterministic, may require validation human 👤 Human involvement Manual review, approval, or input external ☁️ External services API calls, third-party services tool 🔧 Tool invocations Function calls, utilities

docs.title: Data Ports
docs.text:
Entities can define input and output data ports for explicit data flow modeling:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "transform",
      "name": "Transform Step",
      "step_type": "llm",
      "inputs": [
        {
          "name": "raw_data",
          "kind": "object",
          "required": true,
          "description": "Raw input data to transform"
        }
      ],
      "outputs": [
        {
          "name": "processed_data",
          "kind": "object",
          "description": "Transformed output data"
        },
        {
          "name": "audit_log",
          "kind": "file",
          "sensitive": true,
          "description": "Processing audit trail"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Data Port Fields
docs.text: Field Type Required Description name string Yes Port identifier kind enum Yes Data type classification description string No Port description required boolean No Whether input is required (default: false) sensitive boolean No Contains sensitive data (default: false) schema string No JSON Schema reference for validation

docs.title: Data Port Kinds
docs.text: Kind Icon Description file 📄 File-based data object 📦 In-memory object/struct api 🌐 API request/response database 🗄️ Database record/query queue 📬 Message queue item stream 🌊 Streaming data

docs.title: Processing Configuration
docs.text:
The processing field configures step execution characteristics:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "llm_step",
      "name": "LLM Processing",
      "step_type": "llm",
      "processing": {
        "engine": "claude-3-opus",
        "deterministic": false,
        "timeout": "PT30S",
        "cache_key": "input_hash",
        "max_retries": 3
      }
    }
  ]
}
Field Type Description engine string Processing engine identifier deterministic boolean Whether output is deterministic timeout string ISO 8601 duration (e.g., "PT30S") cache_key string Cache key expression max_retries integer Maximum retry attempts

docs.title: Failure Modes
docs.text:
The failure_modes field documents potential failure scenarios:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "external_api",
      "name": "External API Call",
      "step_type": "external",
      "failure_modes": [
        {
          "id": "timeout",
          "name": "Request Timeout",
          "severity": "medium",
          "recovery": "Retry with exponential backoff"
        },
        {
          "id": "rate_limit",
          "name": "Rate Limited",
          "severity": "low",
          "recovery": "Wait and retry"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
Field Type Required Description id string Yes Failure mode identifier name string Yes Human-readable name description string No Detailed description severity enum No critical, high, medium, low recovery string No Recovery strategy description

docs.title: Retry Strategy
docs.text:
The retry_strategy field configures automatic retry behavior:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "api_call",
      "name": "API Call",
      "step_type": "external",
      "retry_strategy": {
        "max_attempts": 3,
        "initial_delay": "PT1S",
        "max_delay": "PT30S",
        "backoff_multiplier": 2.0,
        "retryable_errors": ["timeout", "rate_limit"]
      }
    }
  ]
}
Field Type Description max_attempts integer Maximum retry attempts initial_delay string Initial delay (ISO 8601 duration) max_delay string Maximum delay between retries backoff_multiplier number Exponential backoff multiplier retryable_errors array Error types that trigger retry

docs.title: Process Spec Example
docs.text:
Complete ETL pipeline example:

{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "etl-pipeline",
    "name": "ETL Pipeline",
    "kind": "process",
    "description": "Extract, transform, and load data pipeline"
  },
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "extract",
      "name": "Extract",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "deterministic",
      "outputs": [
        {"name": "raw_data", "kind": "object"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "transform",
      "name": "Transform",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "llm",
      "inputs": [
        {"name": "raw_data", "kind": "object", "required": true}
      ],
      "outputs": [
        {"name": "processed_data", "kind": "object"}
      ],
      "processing": {
        "engine": "claude-3-opus",
        "deterministic": false,
        "timeout": "PT60S"
      }
    },
    {
      "id": "validate",
      "name": "Human Review",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "human",
      "inputs": [
        {"name": "processed_data", "kind": "object", "required": true}
      ],
      "outputs": [
        {"name": "approved_data", "kind": "object"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "load",
      "name": "Load",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "external",
      "inputs": [
        {"name": "approved_data", "kind": "object", "required": true}
      ],
      "failure_modes": [
        {"id": "connection_error", "name": "Connection Error", "severity": "high"}
      ],
      "retry_strategy": {
        "max_attempts": 3,
        "initial_delay": "PT5S",
        "backoff_multiplier": 2.0
      }
    }
  ],
  "flows": [
    {"from": "extract", "to": "transform", "action": "send_data"},
    {"from": "transform", "to": "validate", "action": "review"},
    {"from": "validate", "to": "load", "action": "approve"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Process Spec Security Analysis
docs.text:
PIDL includes security rules specific to process specifications:

Rule Severity Description SEC011 Medium LLM step without downstream validation SEC012 High Sensitive data flows to LLM step SEC013 Medium Non-deterministic step in critical path SEC014 Low External step without failure modes SEC015 Medium Human step without timeout

docs.title: Design: SVG Renderer with Animation Support
docs.text: Status: Draft Author: John Wang Created: 2025-05-17 Last Updated: 2025-05-17

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Add SVG rendering capabilities to PIDL, including static sequence diagrams, animated flow visualizations with moving dots, and network boundary diagrams. This extends the existing render/ package to output self-contained SVG files with optional CSS animations.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Current PIDL renderers output text-based diagram formats (Mermaid, PlantUML, D2, Dot) that require external tools to render. Direct SVG output provides:

  1. Self-contained output - No external rendering tools needed
  2. Animation support - CSS-based flow animations (moving dots) for visualizing data flow
  3. Network boundary views - Architecture diagrams showing trust boundaries and network segments
  4. Embeddable - Works in HTML documents, datasheets, presentations
  5. Themeable - CSS custom properties for light/dark themes
  6. Print-friendly - Static fallback for print media

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Protocol datasheets with embedded diagrams
  • Documentation with animated flow visualizations
  • Architecture diagrams showing network boundaries
  • LinkedIn/social media posts with animated protocol flows
  • Interactive documentation

docs.title: Proposed Formats
docs.text:
Extend render.Format with three new SVG variants:

Format Output Description svg Static SVG Sequence diagram similar to Mermaid output svg-animated Animated SVG Sequence diagram with CSS animations (moving dots) svg-network Network SVG Architecture diagram with boundaries and components 
const (
    FormatSVG         Format = "svg"
    FormatSVGAnimated Format = "svg-animated"
    FormatSVGNetwork  Format = "svg-network"
)

docs.title: Renderer Interface
docs.text:
The new renderers implement the existing Renderer interface:

type SVGRenderer struct {
    // Animated enables CSS animations (moving dots along message lines)
    Animated bool

    // Theme selects color scheme ("light", "dark", "auto")
    Theme string

    // Width sets the SVG width (default: auto-calculated)
    Width int

    // ParticipantSpacing sets horizontal spacing between participants
    ParticipantSpacing int

    // MessageSpacing sets vertical spacing between messages
    MessageSpacing int

    // ShowPhases renders phase boxes as background regions
    ShowPhases bool

    // AnimationDuration sets the flow animation duration (default: 2s)
    AnimationDuration time.Duration

    // AnimationStagger staggers animation start times per message
    AnimationStagger bool
}

type SVGNetworkRenderer struct {
    // Animated enables CSS animations
    Animated bool

    // Theme selects color scheme
    Theme string

    // Boundaries defines network boundary regions
    // If empty, auto-detected from entity metadata
    Boundaries []NetworkBoundary

    // Layout algorithm ("horizontal", "vertical", "auto")
    Layout string
}

type NetworkBoundary struct {
    ID       string
    Name     string
    Entities []string  // entity IDs within this boundary
    Style    string    // "trusted", "dmz", "external"
}

    @keyframes flow {

      100% { offset-distance: 100%; }

docs.title: CSS Offset Path Animation
docs.text:
Use CSS offset-path to animate dots along message paths:

@keyframes flow {
  0% { offset-distance: 0%; }
  100% { offset-distance: 100%; }
}

.flow-dot {
  offset-rotate: 0deg;
  animation: flow var(--animation-duration, 2s) linear infinite;
}

/* Staggered animation delays */
.flow-dot[data-step="1"] { animation-delay: 0s; }
.flow-dot[data-step="2"] { animation-delay: 0.5s; }
.flow-dot[data-step="3"] { animation-delay: 1s; }

docs.text: Option Description Default --animation-duration Total animation cycle time 2s --dot-size Radius of animated dots 4px --dot-color Dot fill color var(--color-accent) stagger Delay between message animations 0.5s direction forward, reverse, alternate forward

docs.text:

    offset-distance: 50%;
  }
}

docs.title: Network Boundaries
docs.text: Network boundaries group entities into logical regions (trust zones, network segments, deployment environments). The renderer supports both automatic inference and explicit configuration.

docs.title: Inference + Override Model
docs.text:
Boundaries follow a layered approach:

  1. Inference (default): If entities have metadata.network, group them automatically
  2. Override: Explicit metadata.networks section takes precedence
  3. CLI override: --boundary flags override everything

This allows sensible defaults while giving humans/LLMs full control when needed.

docs.title: Per-Message Animation Control
docs.text: Animation can be configured globally and overridden per-flow (message). This enables highlighting critical paths, color-coding by outcome, or keeping setup flows static.

docs.title: Flow Animation Schema
docs.text:
Extend the PIDL flow schema with optional animation field:

{
  "flows": [
    {
      "from": "agent",
      "to": "idp",
      "label": "1. Request ID-JAG",
      "animation": {
        "enabled": true,
        "duration": "1.5s",
        "dot_color": "#3182ce",
        "dot_size": 5
      }
    },
    {
      "from": "idp",
      "to": "agent",
      "label": "2. Return ID-JAG",
      "mode": "response",
      "animation": {
        "enabled": true,
        "dot_color": "#68d391",
        "delay": "0.5s"
      }
    },
    {
      "from": "agent",
      "to": "resource",
      "label": "3. Access API",
      "animation": {
        "enabled": true,
        "dot_color": "#3182ce"
      }
    },
    {
      "from": "resource",
      "to": "agent",
      "label": "4. 403 Forbidden",
      "mode": "response",
      "animation": {
        "enabled": true,
        "dot_color": "#fc8181",
        "pulse": true
      }
    },
    {
      "from": "human",
      "to": "agent",
      "label": "Setup: Delegate task",
      "animation": {
        "enabled": false
      }
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "animation": {
      "default_enabled": true,
      "default_duration": "2s",
      "default_dot_color": "#3182ce",
      "stagger": "0.3s",
      "loop": true
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Animation Properties
docs.text: Property Type Default Description enabled boolean true Enable/disable animation for this flow duration string "2s" Animation cycle duration delay string "0s" Start delay (for sequencing) dot_color string theme accent Dot fill color dot_size number 4 Dot radius in pixels dot_shape string "circle" Shape: circle, square, diamond, arrow pulse boolean false Add pulsing effect (for errors/warnings) trail boolean false Show fading trail behind dot direction string "forward" forward, reverse, alternate easing string "linear" CSS easing: linear, ease-in-out, etc.

docs.title: Semantic Presets
docs.text:
For convenience, use semantic presets:

{
  "flows": [
    {
      "from": "agent", "to": "resource",
      "label": "API Call",
      "animation": "request"
    },
    {
      "from": "resource", "to": "agent",
      "label": "Success",
      "animation": "success"
    },
    {
      "from": "resource", "to": "agent",
      "label": "Error",
      "animation": "error"
    },
    {
      "from": "human", "to": "agent",
      "label": "Background",
      "animation": "none"
    }
  ]
}

Preset definitions:

Preset Color Effect Use Case request Blue Standard Outgoing requests response Gray Dashed path Return values success Green Standard Successful operations error Red Pulse Errors, failures warning Orange Pulse Warnings highlight Yellow Glow + larger dot Critical path background Gray, 50% opacity Subtle Setup/teardown none N/A Static arrow No animation

docs.text:
Set defaults in protocol metadata:

  "metadata": {
    "animation": {
      "default_enabled": true,
      "default_duration": "2s",
      "stagger": "0.3s",
      "stagger_mode": "sequential",
      "loop": true,
      "pause_on_hover": true,
      "color_scheme": {
        "request": "#3182ce",
        "response": "#a0aec0",
        "success": "#68d391",
        "error": "#fc8181",
        "warning": "#f6ad55"

docs.text: Mode Description sequential Each flow starts after previous ends overlap Flows start with fixed delay, may overlap parallel All flows animate simultaneously phase Flows within same phase animate together

docs.title: Generated CSS Example
docs.text:
For a flow with custom animation:

/* Flow: agent → idp (step 1) */
#flow-1-dot {
  fill: #3182ce;
  r: 5;
  offset-path: path('M150,80 L300,80');
  offset-rotate: 0deg;
  animation: flow-1 1.5s linear infinite;
  animation-delay: 0s;

@keyframes flow-1 {
  0% { offset-distance: 0%; }
  100% { offset-distance: 100%; }

/* Flow: resource → agent (step 4, error) */
#flow-4-dot {
  fill: #fc8181;
  r: 4;
  offset-path: path('M550,140 L150,140');
  animation: flow-4 2s linear infinite, pulse 0.5s ease-in-out infinite;
  animation-delay: 0.9s;
}

  0%, 100% { opacity: 1; transform: scale(1); }
  50% { opacity: 0.7; transform: scale(1.3); }

docs.title: Resolved Questions
docs.text:
1. Should svg-network infer boundaries from entity metadata, or require explicit configuration?

Resolution: Both. Use inference by default from entity.metadata.network, but allow explicit override via metadata.networks[id].entities or CLI --boundary flags. See Network Boundaries section.

  1. Should we support custom SVG templates for different visual styles?

Resolution: Yes. Support built-in templates (default, sketch, minimal, etc.) and custom templates from directories. Templates include SVG structure, CSS styling, and layout config. See Custom SVG Templates section.

  1. Should animation be configurable per-message (e.g., some flows animate, others don't)?

Resolution: Yes. Each flow can have an animation field with properties like enabled, dot_color, duration, pulse. Also support semantic presets (request, success, error, none). See Per-Message Animation Control section.

docs.title: Extending PIDL
docs.text: This guide explains how to extend PIDL with custom renderers, validation rules, and exporters.

docs.title: Custom Renderers
docs.text: PIDL uses a Renderer interface that you can implement to create custom diagram output formats.

docs.title: The Renderer Interface
docs.text:
package render

import (
    "io"
    "github.com/grokify/pidl"
)

type Renderer interface {
    // Render writes the diagram to the writer.
    Render(w io.Writer, p *pidl.Protocol) error

    // RenderString returns the diagram as a string.
    RenderString(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error)

    // Format returns the output format name.
    Format() Format
}

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Renderer
docs.text:
Here's a complete example of a custom Markdown renderer:

package render

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "strings"

    "github.com/grokify/pidl"
)

// MyMarkdownRenderer generates a custom Markdown format.
type MyMarkdownRenderer struct {
    // Title includes the protocol name as header.
    Title bool
    // ShowDescriptions includes flow descriptions.
    ShowDescriptions bool
}

// NewMyMarkdown creates a new renderer with defaults.
func NewMyMarkdown() *MyMarkdownRenderer {
    return &MyMarkdownRenderer{
        Title:            true,
        ShowDescriptions: true,
    }
}

// Format returns the format identifier.
func (r *MyMarkdownRenderer) Format() Format {
    return Format("my-markdown")
}

// Render writes the Markdown to the writer.
func (r *MyMarkdownRenderer) Render(w io.Writer, p *pidl.Protocol) error {
    s, err := r.RenderString(p)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    _, err = w.Write([]byte(s))
    return err
}

// RenderString returns the Markdown as a string.
func (r *MyMarkdownRenderer) RenderString(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error) {
    var sb strings.Builder

    // Write title
    if r.Title {
        sb.WriteString(fmt.Sprintf("# %s\n\n", p.ProtocolMeta.Name))
    }

    // Write entities
    sb.WriteString("## Entities\n\n")
    for _, e := range p.Entities {
        sb.WriteString(fmt.Sprintf("- **%s** (%s)\n", e.Name, e.Type))
    }
    sb.WriteString("\n")

    // Write flows
    sb.WriteString("## Flows\n\n")
    for i, f := range p.Flows {
        sb.WriteString(fmt.Sprintf("%d. %s → %s: %s\n",
            i+1, f.From, f.To, f.Label))
        if r.ShowDescriptions && f.Description != "" {
            sb.WriteString(fmt.Sprintf("   - %s\n", f.Description))
        }
    }

    return sb.String(), nil
}

docs.title: Registering a Custom Renderer
docs.text:
To integrate your renderer with the render.New() factory:

// In your application code
func init() {
    // Register with the format parser
    render.RegisterFormat("my-markdown", func() render.Renderer {
        return NewMyMarkdown()
    })
}

Or use it directly:

renderer := NewMyMarkdown()
output, err := renderer.RenderString(protocol)

docs.title: Best Practices for Renderers
docs.text:
1. Support configuration options - Use struct fields for customization
  2. Handle both io.Writer and string output - Implement both methods
  3. Check protocol kind - Process specs may need different handling
  4. Handle empty protocols gracefully - Don't panic on missing data
  5. Consider step types - For process specs, use StepType for visual differentiation

docs.title: Custom Validation Rules
docs.text: PIDL's security analysis system uses rules that can be extended.

docs.title: The SecurityRule Structure
docs.text:
type SecurityRule struct {
    // ID is a unique identifier (e.g., "SEC001")
    ID string

    // Name is a human-readable name
    Name string

    // Description explains what the rule checks
    Description string

    // Category groups related rules
    Category string

    // Severity indicates the risk level
    Severity Severity

    // Check is the function that evaluates the rule
    Check func(p *pidl.Protocol, opts *AnalysisOptions) []Risk
}

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Rule
docs.text:
package analyze

import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

// MyCustomRule checks for a specific security pattern.
var MyCustomRule = SecurityRule{
    ID:          "CUSTOM001",
    Name:        "Unencrypted Sensitive Data",
    Description: "Sensitive data should use encryption",
    Category:    CategoryDataProtection,
    Severity:    SeverityHigh,
    Check: func(p *pidl.Protocol, opts *AnalysisOptions) []Risk {
        var risks []Risk

        for _, flow := range p.Flows {
            // Check if flow has sensitive data
            if flow.Annotation != nil && flow.Annotation.DataClassification == "confidential" {
                // Check if encryption is required
                if !hasSecurityRequirement(flow, "encryption") {
                    risks = append(risks, Risk{
                        RuleID:      "CUSTOM001",
                        Severity:    SeverityHigh,
                        Category:    CategoryDataProtection,
                        Location:    fmt.Sprintf("flow %s→%s", flow.From, flow.To),
                        Message:     "Confidential data transmitted without encryption",
                        Remediation: "Add security requirement: encryption",
                    })
                }
            }
        }

        return risks
    },
}

func hasSecurityRequirement(flow pidl.Flow, req string) bool {
    if flow.Security == nil {
        return false
    }
    for _, r := range flow.Security.Requires {
        if r == req {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}

// Add your rule to the analyzer

    analyze.RegisterRule(MyCustomRule)
}

// Or create a custom analyzer
analyzer := analyze.NewAnalyzer()
analyzer.AddRule(MyCustomRule)

results := analyzer.Analyze(protocol)

docs.title: Custom Exporters
docs.text: Workflow exporters convert PIDL process specs to executable formats.

docs.title: The Exporter Pattern
docs.text:
package export

import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

type MyExporter struct {
    // Configuration options
    OutputFormat string
}

func NewMyExporter() *MyExporter {
    return &MyExporter{
        OutputFormat: "default",
    }
}

func (e *MyExporter) Export(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error) {
    // Validate it's a process spec
    if p.ProtocolMeta.Kind != pidl.ProtocolKindProcess {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("only process specs supported")
    }

    // Build your output format
    var sb strings.Builder

    for _, entity := range p.Entities {
        if entity.StepType == "" {
            continue
        }

        // Generate code for this step
        sb.WriteString(e.generateStep(entity))
    }

    return sb.String(), nil
}

func (e *MyExporter) generateStep(entity pidl.Entity) string {
    // Step-type-specific code generation
    switch entity.StepType {
    case pidl.StepTypeDeterministic:
        return fmt.Sprintf("// Deterministic: %s\n", entity.Name)
    case pidl.StepTypeLLM:
        return fmt.Sprintf("// LLM: %s\n", entity.Name)
    case pidl.StepTypeHuman:
        return fmt.Sprintf("// Human: %s\n", entity.Name)
    default:
        return fmt.Sprintf("// Step: %s\n", entity.Name)
    }
}

docs.title: Using Parallel Block Detection
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

func (e *MyExporter) Export(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error) {
    // Detect parallel execution blocks
    blocks := pidl.DetectParallelBlocks(p)

    for _, block := range blocks {
        fmt.Printf("Parallel block: %s\n", block.ID)
        fmt.Printf("  Join condition: %s\n", block.JoinCondition)

        for _, branch := range block.Branches {
            fmt.Printf("  Branch: %s\n", branch.EntityID)
        }
    }

    // Use execution graph for ordering
    graph := pidl.AnalyzeExecutionGraph(p)
    for _, stage := range graph.Stages {
        fmt.Printf("Stage %s: %v\n", stage.ID, stage.Steps)
    }

    return "", nil
}

docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

func (e *MyExporter) Export(p *pidl.Protocol) (string, error) {
    // Analyze costs
    analysis := pidl.AnalyzeProcessCosts(p)

    fmt.Printf("Total estimated cost: $%.4f\n",
        analysis.TotalEstimate.ExpectedCost)

    for stepType, cost := range analysis.CostByType {
        fmt.Printf("  %s: $%.4f\n", stepType, cost)
    }

    return "", nil
}

docs.title: Schema Validation Extension
docs.text: You can extend schema validation with custom validators.

docs.title: Custom Port Validator
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

type CustomValidator struct {
    *pidl.PortSchemaValidator
    customRules []func(port pidl.DataPort, data interface{}) error
}

func NewCustomValidator() *CustomValidator {
    return &CustomValidator{
        PortSchemaValidator: pidl.NewPortSchemaValidator(),
    }
}

func (v *CustomValidator) AddRule(rule func(pidl.DataPort, interface{}) error) {
    v.customRules = append(v.customRules, rule)
}

func (v *CustomValidator) ValidatePortData(port pidl.DataPort, data interface{}) (*pidl.SchemaValidationResult, error) {
    // Run base validation
    result, err := v.PortSchemaValidator.ValidatePortData(port, data)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    // Run custom rules
    for _, rule := range v.customRules {
        if err := rule(port, data); err != nil {
            result.Valid = false
            result.Errors = append(result.Errors, pidl.SchemaValidationError{
                Path:    port.Name,
                Message: err.Error(),
            })
        }
    }

    return result, nil
}

docs.text: Flows are the core semantic unit: directed interactions between entities.

      "from": "client",

      "from": "server",

      "action": "response",

      "mode": "response"

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Flows run in array order. To change the order, move the flow in the array.

The sequence field is deprecated. It is a display-only step number and does not reorder flows. See Ordering in the specification for the rules that apply to entities, phases and scenarios.

docs.title: Conditional Flows
docs.text:
Use condition to specify when a flow executes:

{
  "from": "client",
  "to": "server",
  "action": "refresh_token",
  "condition": "token_expired"
}

Renders as opt block in sequence diagrams.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Add visible notes to flows:

{
  "from": "client",
  "to": "server",
  "action": "authenticate",
  "note": "Requires TLS 1.3"
}

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
For incident attack-flows, a flow can record its evidentiary provenance — how well-substantiated the step is and where it is sourced from. This lets a published attack chain distinguish a step observed in a primary source from one that is inferred.

{
  "from": "agent-collective",
  "to": "hugging-face",
  "action": "exploit_worker",
  "verification": {
    "tier": "corroborated",
    "source": "METR",
    "citation": "https://metr.org/..."
  }
}
Field Type Required Description tier enum Yes reported | corroborated | reproduced | partially_reproduced source string No Originating source (e.g. "OpenAI technical report", "METR") citation string No URL or reference locating the source

The tier vocabulary matches the aisecurity-incidents deepdive.json. Sequence renderers emit a compact provenance badge (e.g. 🔎 corroborated — METR), toggled by the renderer's ShowVerification option, and the security analyzer flags flows below the corroborated tier.

See also:

  • Annotations for typed metadata
  • Alternatives for branching paths

docs.title: PIDL Format
docs.text:
A PIDL document is a JSON file with four sections:

{
  "protocol": { ... },
  "entities": [ ... ],
  "phases": [ ... ],
  "flows": [ ... ]
}
Section Required Description protocol Yes Metadata about the protocol entities Yes Participants in the protocol (min 2) phases No Logical grouping of flows flows Yes Interactions between entities (min 1)

docs.title: Phases
docs.text: Phases provide logical grouping of flows for readability and diagram organization.

docs.title: Basic Phases
docs.text:
{
  "phases": [
    {
      "id": "authorization",
      "name": "Authorization",
      "description": "User authentication and consent"
    },
    {
      "id": "token_exchange",
      "name": "Token Exchange",
      "description": "Exchange code for tokens"
    }
  ]
}

docs.text: Field Type Required Description id string Yes Unique identifier name string Yes Human-readable name description string No Phase description parent string No Parent phase ID for nesting

docs.title: Nested Phases
docs.text:
Phases support hierarchical nesting via the parent field:

{
  "phases": [
    {"id": "auth", "name": "Authentication"},
    {"id": "login", "name": "Login", "parent": "auth"},
    {"id": "mfa", "name": "Multi-Factor Auth", "parent": "auth"},
    {"id": "token", "name": "Token Exchange"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Hierarchy Rules
docs.text:
• A phase with no parent is a root phase
  • A phase with a parent must reference a valid phase ID
  • Circular references are not allowed
  • A phase cannot be its own parent

docs.title: Assigning Flows to Phases
docs.text:
Reference the phase ID in flows:

{
  "flows": [
    {"from": "client", "to": "server", "action": "login", "phase": "login"},
    {"from": "server", "to": "client", "action": "mfa_challenge", "phase": "mfa"},
    {"from": "client", "to": "server", "action": "token_request", "phase": "token"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Process Specifications
docs.text: PIDL supports two profiles: protocol (default) and process. This guide explains when to use each and how to model process workflows.

docs.title: Protocol vs Process
docs.text: Aspect Protocol Process Focus System interactions Data transformations Entities Services, actors, systems Processing steps Flows Request/response patterns Data flow between steps Primary concern "Who talks to whom" "How data transforms" Output Sequence diagrams Pipeline diagrams

docs.title: When to Use Protocol
docs.text:
Use the protocol profile when modeling:

  • Authentication/authorization flows (OAuth, OIDC, SAML)
  • API choreography between services
  • Agent protocols (MCP, A2A)
  • Multi-party interactions with clear request/response patterns
  • Trust relationships between systems

Example: OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, MCP tool invocation.

docs.title: When to Use Process
docs.text:
Use the process profile when modeling:

  • Data pipelines (ETL, data processing)
  • AI/ML workflows with LLM steps
  • Document processing workflows
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Approval workflows with human review

Example: Document extraction → LLM transformation → human review → database load.

docs.title: Defining a Process Spec
docs.text:
Set kind: "process" in the protocol metadata:

{
  "protocol": {
    "id": "document-pipeline",
    "name": "Document Processing Pipeline",
    "kind": "process"
  }
}

docs.title: Step Types
docs.text:
Each entity in a process spec should have a step_type:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "extract",
      "name": "Extract Data",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "deterministic"
    },
    {
      "id": "summarize",
      "name": "LLM Summarization",
      "type": "server",
      "step_type": "llm"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Step Type Reference
docs.text: Step Type When to Use Rendering deterministic Predictable transformations, parsing, validation ⚙️ Blue rectangle llm AI/ML processing, text generation, embeddings 🧠 Purple hexagon human Manual review, approval, data entry 👤 Green circle external API calls, third-party services ☁️ Orange cloud tool Function calls, utility operations 🔧 Gray diamond

docs.title: Data Ports
docs.text:
Define explicit inputs and outputs for each step:

{
  "id": "transform",
  "name": "Transform Step",
  "step_type": "llm",
  "inputs": [
    {
      "name": "raw_document",
      "kind": "file",
      "required": true,
      "description": "PDF or text document to process"
    }
  ],
  "outputs": [
    {
      "name": "summary",
      "kind": "object",
      "description": "Structured summary of the document"
    },
    {
      "name": "embeddings",
      "kind": "object",
      "sensitive": false,
      "description": "Vector embeddings for search"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Port Kinds
docs.text: Kind Icon Use For file 📄 Documents, images, binary data object 📦 JSON objects, structs, in-memory data api 🌐 API request/response payloads database 🗄️ Database records, query results queue 📬 Message queue items stream 🌊 Streaming data, real-time feeds

docs.title: Processing Configuration
docs.text:
Configure execution characteristics:

{
  "id": "llm_step",
  "step_type": "llm",
  "processing": {
    "engine": "claude-3-opus",
    "deterministic": false,
    "timeout": "PT60S",
    "cache_key": "document_hash"
  }
}

docs.title: Failure Handling
docs.text:
Document failure modes and retry strategies:

{
  "id": "api_call",
  "step_type": "external",
  "failure_modes": [
    {
      "id": "timeout",
      "name": "Request Timeout",
      "severity": "medium",
      "recovery": "Retry with exponential backoff"
    }
  ],
  "retry_strategy": {
    "max_attempts": 3,
    "initial_delay": "PT1S",
    "backoff_multiplier": 2.0
  }
}

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Process specs trigger additional security analysis rules:

Rule Severity Issue SEC011 Medium LLM step without downstream validation SEC012 High Sensitive data flows to LLM step SEC013 Medium Non-deterministic step in critical path SEC014 Low External step without failure modes SEC015 Medium Human step without timeout

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Validate LLM outputs - Add a validation step after LLM processing
  2. Mark sensitive data - Use sensitive: true on ports containing PII
  3. Define failure modes - Document how external steps can fail
  4. Set timeouts - Human steps should have timeouts to prevent blocking
  5. Use deterministic steps - For critical path operations that must be reproducible

docs.title: Go Library Usage
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl"

// Check if protocol is a process spec
if p.IsProcessSpec() {
    // Get process steps
    steps := p.ProcessSteps()

    // Filter by step type
    llmSteps := p.LLMSteps()
    humanSteps := p.HumanSteps()

    // Check individual entities
    for _, e := range p.Entities {
        if e.IsLLMStep() {
            // Handle LLM step
        }

        // Get required inputs
        required := e.RequiredInputs()

        // Check for sensitive data
        sensitiveInputs := e.SensitiveInputs()
        sensitiveOutputs := e.SensitiveOutputs()
    }
}

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
Most protocols have more than one journey through the same roles. AAuth has five access modes, from agent identity to federated authorization. OAuth has several grants. Scenarios let one PIDL file describe all of them with one shared list of roles, so every diagram, table and outline generated from the file shows roles and journeys in the same order.

The built-in aauth_protocol example is used throughout this page:

pidl scenarios aauth_protocol

#   ID                       NAME                           KIND      STEPS  PARTICIPANTS
1   agent-identity           Agent identity                 main          3  ap, agent, resource
2   resource-managed         Resource-managed access (tw... main          8  person, ap, agent, resource
3   person-identity          Person identity                main          4  ap, agent, resource, ps
4   ps-authorization         PS authorization (three-party) main          9  person, ap, agent, resource, ps
5   federated-authorization  Federated authorization (fo... main         11  person, ap, agent, resource, ps, as
6   agent-token              Obtain agent token             fragment      2  ap, agent
7   person-token             Obtain person token            fragment      2  agent, ps
8   consent                  User consent                   fragment      4  person, agent, ps

docs.title: Writing Scenarios
docs.text:
Replace the top-level flows array with a scenarios array. Each scenario has an id, a name and its own flows:

{
  "entities": [
    {"id": "person", "name": "Person", "type": "user"},
    {"id": "agent", "name": "Agent", "type": "agent"},
    {"id": "resource", "name": "Resource", "type": "resource_server"},
    {"id": "ps", "name": "Person Server", "type": "authorization_server"}
  ],
  "scenarios": [
    {
      "id": "agent-identity",
      "name": "Agent identity",
      "flows": [
        {"from": "agent", "to": "resource", "action": "signed_request"},
        {"from": "resource", "to": "agent", "action": "ok", "mode": "response"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Order Comes from the File
docs.text:
Order is never set with numbers. It comes from where things sit in the file:

  • Roles follow the entities array. Diagram columns, tables and outlines all use it. To change the column order of every diagram, move the entity.
  • Scenarios follow the scenarios array, with fragments listed after the main scenarios.
  • Steps follow each scenario's flows array.

A scenario's participants list chooses which roles appear. It never reorders them, and validation reports a list that is out of entities order.

docs.title: Shared Steps: Fragments and Includes
docs.text:
Steps that several scenarios share, such as obtaining a token or asking the person for consent, go in a fragment: a scenario with "fragment": true. Other scenarios insert it with an include step:

{
  "id": "ps-authorization",
  "name": "PS authorization (three-party)",
  "flows": [
    {"include": "agent-token"},
    {"include": "person-token"},
    {"from": "agent", "to": "resource", "action": "authorize"},
    {"include": "consent"}
  ]
}

Diagrams draw an include as a labeled box across the fragment's participants. Use --expand to show the fragment's steps in place instead.

docs.title: Generating Output
docs.text:
# One scenario
pidl generate -f mermaid --scenario ps-authorization aauth_protocol

# One scenario with fragments shown step by step
pidl generate -f mermaid --scenario ps-authorization --expand aauth_protocol

# Every main scenario: 01-agent-identity.svg, 02-resource-managed.svg, ...
pidl generate -f svg --all-scenarios -o diagrams/ aauth_protocol

# Add the fragments after the main scenarios: ... 06-agent-token.svg
pidl generate -f svg --all-scenarios --include-fragments -o diagrams/ aauth_protocol

File numbers match the # column of pidl scenarios, so a sorted file listing, a slide deck and the scenario list agree.

Some outputs describe the whole file rather than one scenario:

Format Output scenario-matrix Markdown table of roles by scenario. ● takes part directly, ○ takes part only through an included fragment token-table Markdown table of tokens: issuer, audience, binding, who checks each token, which claims they rely on, and the scenarios that issue and check it outline Markdown outline of roles, scenarios with numbered steps, and tokens, as a starting point for guides and slide decks outline-json The same outline as JSON, for deck and guide tooling 
pidl generate -f scenario-matrix aauth_protocol
pidl generate -f outline -o aauth-outline.md aauth_protocol

simulate and debug take --scenario and run the scenario with fragments expanded.

docs.title: Recording Who Checks What
docs.text:
Token definitions can list who checks each token and which claims they rely on. Flow security can say which tokens a step issues and checks, and who signs the request:

{
  "metadata": {
    "tokens": [
      {
        "id": "resource_token",
        "issuer": "resource",
        "verified_by": ["ps", "as"],
        "claims": [
          {"name": "agent_jkt", "checked_by": ["ps", "as"],
           "description": "Thumbprint of the agent's key, compared with the key that signed the request"}
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

{"from": "resource", "to": "agent", "action": "challenge", "mode": "response",
 "security": {"issues": ["resource_token"]}}

{"from": "ps", "to": "as", "action": "federate",
 "security": {"requires": ["signature"], "verifies": ["resource_token"]}}

With these fields, pidl analyze follows each token through a scenario:

Rule Reports SEC017 A role that no flow uses SEC018 A step that checks a token before any earlier step issues it SEC019 A request signed by someone other than its sender, or than the entity the presented token was delivered to SEC020 A receiver that checks a token without being listed in its verified_by SEC021 A fragment that no scenario includes

In the AAuth example, SEC019 flags federated access: the PS signs the request to the AS, but the resource token it presents was delivered to the agent, so a check of agent_jkt against the signing key would compare against the PS's key.

pidl analyze aauth_protocol                                      # whole file
pidl analyze --scenario federated-authorization aauth_protocol   # one scenario

docs.title: Composing Files
docs.text:
extends and imports understand scenarios:

  • extends keeps the base file's scenario order. A scenario with the same id in the derived file replaces the base one in place; new scenarios follow. exclude_scenarios removes base scenarios.
  • imports can bring in selected scenarios with "scenarios": ["id", ...]. The fragments they include come with them, and alias prefixes every ID they reference.
  • When composition leaves a file with both top-level flows and scenarios, the flows become the first scenario, named after the protocol.

docs.title: Comparing Versions
docs.text:
pidl diff matches scenarios by id. It reports scenarios that were added, removed or renamed, changed steps within each scenario, include steps that point at a different fragment, and roles or scenarios that moved relative to each other.

pidl diff aauth-draft-10.json aauth-draft-11.json

docs.title: In Go
docs.text:
p, err := pidl.ParseFile("aauth.json")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
for _, s := range p.ScenarioSummaries() {
    proj, err := p.Scenario(s.ID, pidl.ProjectOptions{})
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    svg, err := render.RenderString(render.FormatSVG, proj)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    name := fmt.Sprintf("%02d-%s.svg", s.Position, s.ID)
    if err := os.WriteFile(name, []byte(svg), 0o600); err != nil {
        return err
    }
}

Protocol.Outline() returns the ordered outline as Go values, Protocol.Flatten() returns every scenario's flows once, and Protocol.TokenUsage(id) lists the scenarios that issue and check a token.

docs.title: Walkthrough Viewer
docs.text:
The walkthrough viewer turns a PIDL file into a page you can step through, one message at a time. It is built for learning a protocol and for presenting it: pick a scenario, press → and watch the active message, its two roles, and its request and response.

pidl generate -f viewer -o aauth.html aauth_protocol
open aauth.html

The output is one self-contained HTML file. It needs no server and no network, so it can be emailed, attached to an issue or opened straight from disk.

docs.title: The Page
docs.text: Area Shows Menu bar The protocol name, a scenario selector (main scenarios, then shared steps), Overview, ← and →, and the step count Sequence card (left) The scenario's roles and steps. Shared steps (fragments) appear as labeled bands. The active step's arrow and label are highlighted, with its sender outlined in blue and its receiver in green; earlier steps are dimmed and later ones faint. Caption (under the diagram) The active step, the fragments it sits inside, its description and note, and any analyzer findings Request card (upper right) The active request, or the request a response answers Response card (lower right) The response, once you step to it

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Key Action → ↓ Space Page Down Next step ← ↑ Page Up Previous step Home Overview (all steps, none active) End Last step P Present on a 16:9 stage

The URL records the scenario and step, for example #federated-authorization/12, so a link opens at that step.

docs.title: Requests, Responses and Tokens
docs.text:
When a flow has an example, the cards show it:

  • HTTP: the request line, Host, headers in written order and body, or the status line, headers and body. Headers covered by the HTTP message signature (from Signature-Input) are marked signed. Long values such as JWTs shorten; click to expand.
  • Tokens: each decoded token's header and claims. Claims that the receiving role checks, according to the token's claims and checked_by, are highlighted.
  • Provenance: a draft badge for examples taken from the cited source with values aligned, or derived for examples written from its normative text, with the source section and the example's note.

A request's response appears only when you reach it, so the walkthrough reveals each answer in order. A pending response pairs with the poll it answers.

docs.title: Presenting
docs.text: Present (or P) places the page on a fixed 1600×900 stage scaled to the window, letterboxed, so it looks the same on any projector or shared screen. Theme cycles auto, light and dark.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The viewer reads the walkthrough produced by pidl generate -f walkthrough-json: every scenario with fragments expanded, each step's example, and analyzer findings attached to the steps they concern (SEC016, flow provenance, is left out). Use that format to build other viewers.

docs.title: Developing the Viewer
docs.text:
The viewer lives in viewer/ (Vite, React and TypeScript):

cd viewer
npm ci
npm run data       # write public/walkthrough.json from the AAuth example
npm run dev        # http://localhost:5173
npm test
npm run build:embed  # rebuild render/viewer/viewer.html for the Go binary

go generate ./render runs the same build. CI fails when the committed render/viewer/viewer.html does not match a fresh build.

docs.title: Workflow Engine Exports
docs.text: PIDL process specifications can be exported to workflow orchestration platforms for execution. This guide covers the available exporters and how to use them.

docs.title: Supported Platforms
docs.text: Platform Language Export Format Use Case Temporal Go .go Durable workflow orchestration Prefect Python .py Data pipeline orchestration BPMN 2.0 XML .bpmn Standard interchange format AWS Step Functions JSON .json Serverless workflow orchestration

docs.title: Go Library Usage
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/pidl/export"

// Load your process specification
p, _ := pidl.ParseFile("pipeline.pidl.json")

// Export to Temporal
temporal := export.NewTemporalExporter()
goCode, _ := temporal.Export(p)

// Export to Prefect
prefect := export.NewPrefectExporter()
pythonCode, _ := prefect.Export(p)

// Export to BPMN
bpmn := export.NewBPMNExporter()
xml, _ := bpmn.Export(p)

// Export to AWS Step Functions
stepfn := export.NewStepFunctionsExporter()
asl, _ := stepfn.Export(p)

exporter.WorkflowName = "ProcessData"    // Override workflow function name
exporter.IncludeActivities = true        // Generate activity stubs

    "context"
    "time"

        },
    }
    ctx = workflow.WithActivityOptions(ctx, ao)
    // ... workflow logic
}

// Activities with step-type-specific patterns
func ExtractDataActivity(ctx context.Context, input interface{}) (interface{}, error) {
    // External service call pattern for "external" step type
    return input, nil
}

func TransformDataActivity(ctx context.Context, input interface{}) (interface{}, error) {
    // LLM processing pattern for "llm" step type
    return input, nil

docs.title: Prefect Export
docs.text: The Prefect exporter generates Python code with async/sync flow and task definitions.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
exporter := export.NewPrefectExporter()
exporter.FlowName = "process_data"  // Override flow function name
exporter.IncludeTasks = true        // Generate task stubs
exporter.UseAsync = true            // Generate async functions (default)

docs.title: Generated Code Structure
docs.text:
"""
process_data_flow - Generated by PIDL
Source: etl-pipeline
"""

from prefect import flow, task
import asyncio
from typing import Any, Dict

@task(name="Extract Data", tags=["external"])
async def extract_data_task(data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Extract data from source."""
    # External service call pattern
    return data

@task(name="Transform Data", tags=["llm"])
async def transform_data_task(data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Transform data using LLM."""
    # LLM processing pattern
    return data

@flow(name="process_data_flow")
async def process_data_flow(input_data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    ETL Pipeline
    Generated from PIDL process specification: etl-pipeline
    """
    result = input_data
    result = await extract_data_task(result)
    result = await transform_data_task(result)
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(process_data_flow({}))

docs.text:

exporter.UseAsync = false

docs.text:
PIDL parallel blocks are converted to Step Functions Parallel states:

  "parallel_block": {
    "Type": "Parallel",
    "Branches": [
      {
        "StartAt": "branch_a",
        "States": { "branch_a": { "Type": "Task", "End": true } }
      },

docs.title: 1. Define Step Types
docs.text:
Always set step_type on process entities for accurate export:

{
  "id": "validate",
  "name": "Validate Input",
  "step_type": "deterministic"
}

docs.title: 2. Add Retry Strategies
docs.text:
Configure retry behavior in PIDL for it to be reflected in exports:

{
  "id": "api_call",
  "step_type": "external",
  "retry_strategy": {
    "max_attempts": 3,
    "initial_delay": "1s",
    "backoff_multiplier": 2.0
  }
}

docs.title: 3. Set Timeouts
docs.text:
Define processing timeouts for proper timeout handling:

{
  "id": "llm_step",
  "step_type": "llm",
  "processing": {
    "timeout": "300s"
  }
}

docs.title: 4. Use Descriptive Names
docs.text:
Entity names become activity/task names in generated code:

{
  "id": "extract_customer_data",
  "name": "Extract Customer Data from CRM"
}

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Generated code contains stubs that need implementation
  • Parallel blocks require manual configuration in some platforms
  • Complex conditional logic may need manual adjustment
  • Human approval patterns vary by platform

import "github.com/grokify/pidl"
