docs.title: Parallel Execution Modeling
docs.text:
Model parallel execution patterns in process specifications:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "fork_point",
      "name": "Fork",
      "step_type": "parallel",
      "parallel": {
        "mode": "fork_join",
        "join_condition": "all",
        "branches": [
          {"id": "b1", "entity_id": "worker_1"},
          {"id": "b2", "entity_id": "worker_2"}
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}

// Analyze execution graph
graph := pidl.AnalyzeExecutionGraph(protocol)

// Get execution stages (parallelizable groups)
for _, stage := range graph.Stages {
    fmt.Printf("Stage %s: %v\n", stage.ID, stage.Steps)
}

// Find critical path
fmt.Println("Critical path:", graph.CriticalPath)

// Check if two entities can run in parallel
if pidl.CanExecuteInParallel(protocol, "stepA", "stepB") {
    // Execute concurrently
}

// Get maximum parallelism
maxParallel := pidl.GetMaxParallelism(protocol)

Parallel modes:

Mode Description fork_join Execute branches in parallel, wait for all race Execute branches in parallel, first wins scatter Distribute work across instances gather Collect results from parallel branches

docs.title: Cost Tracking
docs.text:
Estimate and track execution costs for process specifications:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "llm_step",
      "step_type": "llm",
      "processing": {
        "cost_model": {
          "type": "token_based",
          "input_token_cost": 0.003,
          "output_token_cost": 0.015,
          "estimated_input_tokens": 1000,
          "estimated_output_tokens": 500,
          "cost_unit": "USD"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

// Analyze process costs
analysis := pidl.AnalyzeProcessCosts(protocol)

// Total estimated cost
fmt.Printf("Expected cost: $%.4f\n", analysis.TotalEstimate.ExpectedCost)

// Cost by step type
for stepType, cost := range analysis.CostByType {
    fmt.Printf("%s: $%.4f\n", stepType, cost)
}

// Calculate actual execution cost
metrics := pidl.ExecutionMetrics{
    InputTokens:  1500,
    OutputTokens: 750,
    Duration:     30 * time.Second,
}
actualCost := pidl.CalculateExecutionCost(entity, metrics)

Cost model types:

Type Description fixed Fixed cost per execution token_based Cost based on input/output tokens time_based Cost based on execution duration api_call Cost per API call hybrid Combined cost factors

docs.title: Latency Budget Tracking
docs.text:
Define timing SLIs (Service Level Indicators) for process steps:

{
  "entities": [
    {
      "id": "llm_step",
      "step_type": "llm",
      "processing": {
        "latency_budget": {
          "p50": "2s",
          "p95": "8s",
          "p99": "15s",
          "max": "30s",
          "variance_class": "high"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

// Analyze process latency
analysis := pidl.AnalyzeProcessLatency(protocol)

// Total latency estimates
fmt.Printf("P50: %s, P95: %s, P99: %s\n",
    analysis.TotalLatency.P50,
    analysis.TotalLatency.P95,
    analysis.TotalLatency.P99)

// Critical path latency
fmt.Printf("Critical path: %v\n", analysis.CriticalPath)
fmt.Printf("Critical path P50: %s\n", analysis.CriticalPathLatency.P50)

// Parallel savings
fmt.Printf("Parallel savings: %s\n", analysis.ParallelSavings)

// Budget violations
for _, v := range analysis.BudgetViolations {
    fmt.Printf("%s: %s exceeded (budget: %s, estimated: %s)\n",
        v.EntityID, v.Metric, v.Budget, v.Estimated)
}

// Measure actual execution
measurement := pidl.CalculateActualLatency(entity, 5*time.Second)
if measurement.ExceedsP95 {
    // Handle SLI violation
}

Variance classes:

Class Description low Consistent, predictable latency (deterministic steps) medium Moderate variance (external APIs, tools) high High variance (LLM, human tasks)

if !result.Valid {

}

docs.title: PIDL v0.6.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-09-13

This release adds flow verification provenance for incident attack-flows — a way to record how well-substantiated each step is and where it is sourced from — along with renderer badges and an analyzer rule, plus a comprehensive AIDLC workflow process-specification example.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Flow.Verification records evidentiary provenance: a verification tier, source, and citation

  • A security-analysis rule flags flows below the corroborated tier
  • New comprehensive AIDLC workflow process-specification example

docs.title: Flow Verification Provenance
docs.text:
Record where an attack-flow step comes from and how well-substantiated it is:

{
  "from": "agent-collective",
  "to": "hugging-face",
  "action": "exploit_worker",
  "verification": {
    "tier": "corroborated",
    "source": "METR",

  }
}

  • The schema addition is additive and backward-compatible

See the Flows guide and Specification.

docs.title: PIDL v0.7.0 Release Notes
docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-10-19

This release lets one PIDL file describe a whole protocol: its roles and an ordered list of scenarios, with shared steps written once as fragments. Every output follows the file's order, so diagrams, tables, outlines and the slide decks and guides built from them agree. It also brings the fixes prepared since v0.6.0: D2 sequence diagrams, deterministic SVG output, and Windows builds.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Scenarios: named journeys through the same roles, such as AAuth's five access modes, in one file
  • Fragments and include steps: shared steps drawn as labeled boxes in PlantUML, Mermaid, D2 and SVG, or expanded in place
  • Consistent ordering: the entities and scenarios arrays set the order of every output
  • Overview outputs: roles-by-scenario matrix, token table, and an ordered outline in Markdown and JSON
  • Token verification: record who checks each token and claim and who signs each request; new analyzer rules follow tokens through a scenario
  • AAuth example: draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-11 with its five access modes

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
{
  "scenarios": [
    {
      "id": "ps-authorization",
      "name": "PS authorization (three-party)",
      "flows": [
        {"include": "person-token"},
        {"from": "agent", "to": "resource", "action": "authorize"},
        {"include": "consent"}
      ]
    },
    {"id": "consent", "name": "User consent", "fragment": true, "flows": [ ... ]}
  ]
}

A file has either flows, which works exactly as before, or scenarios. See the Scenarios guide and the specification.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text: Command What it does pidl scenarios <file> Lists scenarios in output order generate --scenario <id> Renders one scenario generate --all-scenarios -o <dir> Writes 01-<id>.svg, 02-<id>.svg, … in file order generate --expand Shows included fragments step by step generate -f scenario-matrix Roles by scenario generate -f token-table Tokens, checkers, claims and the scenarios that use them generate -f outline / outline-json Ordered outline for guides and decks simulate, debug, analyze --scenario <id> Work on one scenario

docs.title: Token Verification and Analysis
docs.text:
Token definitions gain verified_by and claims; flow security gains signed_by, issues and verifies. New rules:

Rule Reports SEC017 A role that no flow uses SEC018 A token checked before any earlier step issues it SEC019 A request signed by someone other than its sender or the token holder SEC020 A token checked by an entity not in its verified_by SEC021 A fragment that no scenario includes

In the AAuth example, SEC019 flags federated access, where the PS signs the request to the AS while presenting a resource token delivered to the agent.

docs.title: Composition and Diff
docs.text: extends and imports merge scenarios, with exclude_scenarios and an import scenarios selector. pidl diff compares scenarios by ID and reports roles and scenarios that moved.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text:
• Network boundary diagrams list entities in entities order instead of alphabetically. Sort the entities array to keep the previous layout.
  • Flow.sequence is deprecated. It is a display-only step number and never affected order.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• D2 sequence diagrams render messages as edges, with quoted labels and correct response direction
  • Network and trust SVG output, network boundary assignment and pidl diff output no longer depend on map iteration order
  • Labeled process flows link one output to one input instead of every input
  • Windows checkouts use LF line endings, so embedded SVG templates and golden tests match other platforms
  • CLI components and trust no longer crash without a metadata block; the debugger no longer loops at end of input

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Existing files need no changes. To adopt scenarios, move the top-level flows into a scenario:

{"scenarios": [{"id": "main", "name": "Main flow", "flows": [ ... ]}]}

docs.text:
Release Date: 2026-10-19

This release turns a PIDL file into a walkthrough you can present. pidl generate -f viewer writes one self-contained HTML page that steps through each scenario one message at a time: the active roles and message are highlighted on the sequence diagram, a narrative explains the step, and the request and response appear beside it with their headers, bodies and decoded tokens. The page needs no server, so it can be shared as a file.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Walkthrough viewer for any PIDL protocol, with presentation controls and a 16:9 presentation mode
  • Flow examples: illustrative requests, responses and decoded tokens, each citing its source
  • A fully worked AAuth draft-11 example with narratives and consistent example values throughout

docs.title: Walkthrough Viewer
docs.text:
pidl generate -f viewer -o aauth.html aauth_protocol
Area Shows Menu bar Protocol name, scenario selector, theme, Present Sequence card Scenario introduction, the diagram with shared steps as labeled bands, the active step's narrative, and Overview, back, Step n / total and forward controls Request and response cards Request line, Host, headers and body; status, headers and body. Signed headers are marked; a Tokens tab decodes each token and highlights the claims the receiver checks

Keys: → and ← step, Home and End jump, P presents on a 16:9 stage. The URL records the scenario and step. See the Walkthrough Viewer guide.

docs.title: Flow Examples
docs.text: A flow's example holds a request, a response and decoded tokens, with a source citation and a kind: draft (taken from the source, values aligned to the scenario) or derived (written from its normative text). See the specification.

docs.title: Walkthrough Data
docs.text: generate -f walkthrough-json writes the data the viewer renders: every scenario with fragments expanded, each step's example and narrative, and analyzer findings attached to the steps they concern. Use it to build other viewers.

docs.title: AAuth Example
docs.text: Every step of the five access modes and the agent token, person token and consent fragments has a narrative and an example. Values are shared throughout: one agent key whose thumbprint is the resource token's agent_jkt, one person, and one timeline within the draft's token lifetimes. The agent token step follows the web app pattern of the AAuth Bootstrap guidance.

docs.text: • For files with scenarios, analyzer findings from flow rules now point at the written scenario flow instead of an index into the flattened protocol.

docs.title: Process Spec Profile - Product Requirements Document
docs.text: Feature: Process Spec Profile for PIDL Version: 1.0 Status: Draft Author: Generated from IDEATION_PROCESSSPEC.md analysis

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Extend PIDL to support Process Spec - a profile for describing workflow and process semantics. This enables PIDL to model not just protocol choreography but also data pipelines, AI/LLM workflows, and multi-step processes with rich node semantics.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Current PIDL excels at describing "who talks to whom, in what order" for protocols like OAuth and MCP. However, modern systems require describing:

  • Data pipelines - ETL/ELT with deterministic transformations
  • AI/LLM workflows - Non-deterministic processing with model policies
  • Multi-step processes - VisionSpec-style document generation flows
  • Hybrid processes - Mixing deterministic validation with LLM generation

Users currently must use separate tools (BPMN, custom YAML) to describe these workflows, losing the benefits of PIDL's diagram generation, validation, and analysis capabilities.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. G1: Enable PIDL to describe process/workflow semantics without breaking existing protocol support
  2. G2: Support differentiation between deterministic and non-deterministic (LLM) processing steps
  3. G3: Generate the same diagram outputs (PlantUML, Mermaid, D2, SVG) from process specs
  4. G4: Maintain backward compatibility with existing PIDL documents
  5. G5: Enable security analysis and simulation for process flows

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Full BPMN compatibility (use dedicated BPMN tools for that)
  • Code generation for workflow execution engines
  • Runtime execution of processes (simulation only)
  • Process mining or discovery from logs

docs.title: US1: AI Workflow Designer
docs.text:
As an AI systems architect, I want to describe an LLM-powered document generation pipeline so that I can visualize the flow, identify non-deterministic steps, and generate documentation.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • Can define nodes with stepType: llm vs stepType: deterministic
  • Can specify inputs (files, objects, APIs) and outputs
  • Generated diagrams show processing type visually
  • Can run simulation to trace execution

docs.title: US2: Data Pipeline Engineer
docs.text:
As a data engineer, I want to describe ETL pipelines in PIDL so that I can use the same tooling for both API protocols and data flows.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • Can define source, transform, and sink nodes
  • Can specify data lineage through flows
  • Can annotate PII/sensitive data handling
  • DOT/D2 output shows data flow direction

docs.title: US3: VisionSpec User
docs.text:
As a VisionSpec user, I want to describe the MRD → PRD → TRD → Execution Spec pipeline so that I can visualize and validate the document generation process.

Acceptance Criteria:

// ValidateProcess performs process-specific validation.
func (p *Protocol) ValidateProcess() ValidationErrors {
    var errs ValidationErrors

    if p.ProtocolMeta.Kind != ProtocolKindProcess {

    return errs
}

// SEC011: LLM step without output validation
func checkLLMOutputValidation(p *Protocol) []SecurityRisk {
    var risks []SecurityRisk
    for _, e := range p.Entities {
        if e.StepType == StepTypeLLM {
            if !hasDownstreamValidation(p, e.ID) {
                risks = append(risks, SecurityRisk{
                    Rule:     "SEC011",
                    Severity: SeverityMedium,
                    Entity:   e.ID,
                    Message:  "LLM step output not validated by downstream deterministic step",

            }
        }
    }
    return risks
}

func (e *Executor) canExecuteStep(entity *Entity) bool {
    if entity.StepType == "" {
        return true // Not a process step, use default logic

            }
        }
    }
    return true
}

docs.title: PRD — Ordered roles and multiple scenarios per protocol
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-001 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A PIDL file describes one protocol as a list of entities and a single ordered list of flows. Real protocols are not one flow. AAuth, for example, has seven roles, five access modes and about eight shared sub-flows (agent bootstrap, discovery, interaction, deferred response, mission lifecycle, step-up, call chaining, revocation). Documenting it today means one file per flow, tied together with imports or extends. That leaves four gaps:

  1. No shared order. Each file decides its own entity order, and there is no order across flows. A slide deck, a guide and a set of diagrams generated from those files can each present roles and flows in a different sequence.
  2. No reuse inside a flow. A shared sub-flow such as "interaction" has to be copied into every flow that uses it, or left out.
  3. No checks across flows. Validation runs per file, so it cannot report a role that no flow uses or a token that is used before any flow issues it.
  4. No overview outputs. Nothing renders a roles × flows table or a token table for the whole protocol.

Flow.sequence adds confusion: it is documented as "explicit ordering" but no code sorts by it, so its value never affects the output.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• One PIDL file can hold a protocol's roles and an ordered list of named scenarios, each with its own ordered flows.
  • Array position is the only source of order, for roles, scenarios, phases and flows. Every output (diagram, table, outline) shows the same order.
  • A scenario can include another scenario as a reusable fragment, shown as a labeled box or expanded in place.
  • Validation and analysis work across all scenarios in a file.
  • New outputs give an overview of the whole protocol: a roles × scenarios matrix, a token table and an ordered outline that guides and presentations can be built from.
  • Existing files keep working without changes.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Generating slide decks or guides directly. PIDL emits ordered, structured outputs. Deck and guide tools consume them.
  • A "journey" concept tied to human users or UX. Scenarios cover flows with or without a person. A display name can say "journey" where an audience prefers it.
  • Message schemas or transport details. These stay out of scope as stated in the main roadmap.
  • Numeric ordering fields. Order comes from array position only.

docs.title: Users and Stakeholders
docs.text:
• Protocol reviewers who need one diagram per scenario, plus a token table that shows who issues and who checks each token.
  • Developer relations and educators who build presentations and guides and need roles and scenarios in the same order everywhere.
  • Spec authors who track how a draft changes between versions. pidl diff should report scenario-level changes.
  • Tool builders who use the Go library and need a stable API for one scenario at a time.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
1. Scenarios. A protocol file MAY contain a top-level scenarios array. Each scenario has an id, a name, an optional description, an optional participants list, an optional fragment flag and a flows array.
  2. Includes. An entry in a scenario's flows array MAY be an include step ({"include": "<scenario-id>"}) instead of a message.
  3. Ordering rule.
  4. The order of the entities array sets the order of roles everywhere.
  5. The order of the scenarios array sets the order of scenarios.
  6. The order of the phases array sets the order of phases.
  7. The order of flows within a scenario sets the order of messages.
  8. Participants follow entity order. A scenario's participants list selects roles. It never reorders them. A list that is out of order is a validation error.
  9. Default participants. When participants is omitted, a scenario's participants are the entities its flows and includes use, in entities order.
  10. Fragments. A scenario with "fragment": true can be included by other scenarios. Commands that render every scenario skip fragments unless asked to include them.
  11. Backward compatibility.
  12. A file with a top-level flows array and no scenarios behaves exactly as it does today.
  13. A file that has both a non-empty flows array and a scenarios array is invalid.
  14. Single-scenario projection. The library can turn one scenario into a single-flow Protocol, so every existing renderer, the executor and the debugger work on it unchanged.
  15. CLI selection. generate, simulate, debug and analyze accept --scenario <id>.
  16. Rendering every scenario. generate --all-scenarios -o <dir> writes one file per scenario. Each file name starts with a zero-padded position, such as 01-agent-identity.mmd, so sorting the files by name keeps scenario order.
  17. Collapsed includes. By default, a renderer draws an include as a labeled box over the fragment's participants. --expand inlines the fragment's flows instead.
  18. Overview outputs:
    • a roles × scenarios matrix
    • a token table: issuer, audience, binding, who checks it and the claims they rely on
    • an ordered outline (Markdown and JSON) listing roles, then scenarios with their steps
  19. Verification semantics.
    • TokenDefinition records who checks each token and which claims they rely on.
    • FlowSecurity records who signs a request and which tokens the receiver checks.
  20. Checks across scenarios. The analyzer reports:
    • roles used by no scenario
    • tokens checked in a flow before any earlier step issued them
    • flows signed by someone other than the sender, unless annotated
    • token checkers that are not participants of the scenario
  21. Composition.
    • extends and imports merge scenarios by id, base scenarios first.
    • exclude_scenarios removes scenarios from the base.
  22. Diff. pidl diff matches scenarios by id and reports scenarios that were added or removed, changed flows, and changes in the order of roles or scenarios.
  23. Flow.sequence deprecation. The field is documented as display only, and no code may sort by it.
  24. Example. The built-in examples include AAuth, with seven roles, five main scenarios and its shared fragments.

docs.title: Non-Functional
docs.text:
• Deterministic output. The same input always produces identical output. No output order may depend on Go map iteration.
  • No change for existing files. For every existing example, generate output stays byte-for-byte the same.
  • Library first. All behavior lives in the pidl and render packages. The CLI only parses flags and calls them.
  • The JSON Schema in schema/pidl.schema.json describes the new fields and validates every example.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• The AAuth example validates and renders five main scenario diagrams in Mermaid, PlantUML and D2, with roles in the same column order.
  • --all-scenarios output and the outline list scenarios in the same order as the file.
  • The golden-file tests for existing examples pass unchanged.
  • A four-party AAuth scenario annotated with signed_by makes the analyzer report that the PS, not the agent, signs the request to the AS.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Flow index references. exclude_flows and ParallelBranch.flow_refs use indices into the top-level flows array. Inside scenarios they need a scenario scope. Mitigation: index within the scenario, and reject index references that don't say which scenario they mean.
  • Collapsed include rendering differs by format. Mermaid has no ref fragment. Mitigation: use rect plus a note in Mermaid, ref over in PlantUML and a group in D2, and test each with golden files.
  • Schema growth. New optional fields make the format larger. Mitigation: all are optional, and the scenario fields are grouped together in the specification.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• "Scenario" rather than "journey". "Journey" usually means a human user's path through a product. Many protocol scenarios have no person in them (for example agent-to-resource identity). "Scenario" is the common term in specs and testing, and it fits PIDL's simulator ("run scenario four-party"). Display names may still say "journey".
  • Array position is the only order. A second mechanism (numeric order or sequence fields) lets outputs drift apart.
  • Fragments are scenarios. Shared sub-flows use the same type, so the ordering and validation rules need no special cases.
  • Collapsed by default. Presentations and overview diagrams read better with a sub-flow drawn as one labeled box. --expand serves detailed review.

docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-001 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Current State
docs.text:
• Protocol (types.go) has Entities []Entity, Phases []Phase and Flows []Flow. A file describes exactly one flow.
  • Sequence renderers (render/mermaid.go, render/plantuml.go, render/d2.go) declare participants by iterating p.Entities, so column order already follows the array. Each renderer declares every entity, including ones the flow never uses.
  • Flow.Sequence is documented as "explicit ordering". The only place it is read is a non-negative check (validate_flow.go). Nothing sorts by it.
  • ProtocolMetadata.Networks is a map[string]*NetworkConfig. Its order is undefined unless network_layout.order is set.
  • ProtocolExtends.ExcludeFlows and ParallelBranch.FlowRefs are integer indices into Protocol.Flows.
  • Executor and Debugger index into Protocol.Flows directly.
  • render/markdown_matrix.go builds an entities × protocol-roles table and sorts the protocol columns alphabetically.
  • ValidationError has no severity, so every reported problem is an error.

docs.title: 1. Types
docs.text:
// Scenario is a named, ordered sequence of flows within a protocol.
type Scenario struct {
    ID           string   `json:"id"`
    Name         string   `json:"name"`
    Description  string   `json:"description,omitempty"`
    Participants []string `json:"participants,omitempty"` // subset of entity IDs, in entity order
    Fragment     bool     `json:"fragment,omitempty"`     // reusable via include; skipped by --all-scenarios
    Flows        []Flow   `json:"flows"`
}

type Protocol struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    Flows     []Flow     `json:"flows,omitempty"`     // was required; now optional when Scenarios is set
    Scenarios []Scenario `json:"scenarios,omitempty"`
}

type Flow struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    // Include references a scenario whose flows are inserted at this
    // point. When set, From, To and Action must be empty.
    Include string `json:"include,omitempty"`
    // Sequence is a display-only step number. It never affects order.
    // Deprecated: order is the position in the flows array.
    Sequence int `json:"sequence,omitempty"`
}

Verification semantics:

type TokenDefinition struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    VerifiedBy []string     `json:"verified_by,omitempty"` // entity IDs, in entity order
    Claims     []TokenClaim `json:"claims,omitempty"`      // ordered
}

type TokenClaim struct {
    Name        string   `json:"name"`
    CheckedBy   []string `json:"checked_by,omitempty"`
    Description string   `json:"description,omitempty"`
}

type FlowSecurity struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    SignedBy string   `json:"signed_by,omitempty"` // entity ID; defaults to Flow.From
    Issues   []string `json:"issues,omitempty"`    // token IDs carried in the response
    Verifies []string `json:"verifies,omitempty"`  // token IDs the receiver checks
}

type ProtocolExtends struct {
    // ...existing fields...
    ExcludeScenarios []string `json:"exclude_scenarios,omitempty"`
}

Issues and Verifies give the analyzer the data it needs for the "used before issued" check without a full simulation.

docs.title: 2. Ordering rules
docs.text:
These rules are normative in docs/SPECIFICATION.md:

  1. Role order is the order of entities.
  2. Scenario order is the order of scenarios.
  3. Phase order is the order of phases.
  4. Message order within a scenario is the order of its flows. An include expands in place.
  5. Every list derived from these arrays keeps their order. Examples are participants, token checkers, matrix rows and columns, outline entries and generated file names.
  6. Collections keyed by name must be arrays of objects with an id. metadata.networks stays a map for compatibility, but renderers order it by network_layout.order when set and otherwise by first appearance of its entities in entities. They never order it by map iteration.

Helpers in a new file order.go:

func (p *Protocol) EntityIndex(id string) int          // -1 if absent
func (p *Protocol) OrderEntities(ids []string) []string // stable sort by EntityIndex
func (p *Protocol) ScenarioIDs(includeFragments bool) []string

docs.title: 3. Validation (validate_scenario.go)
docs.text:
Added to Protocol.Validate():

  • flows must be non-empty when scenarios is empty, and empty when scenarios is non-empty.
  • Scenario ids are unique and match the existing ID pattern.
  • Every participants entry is an entity ID. The list has no duplicates and is in entity order. Out-of-order lists fail with a message that gives the expected order.
  • Each flow is either an include (only include, plus optional phase, note, condition) or a message (from, to, action). It cannot be both.
  • include targets exist and have fragment: true.
  • Includes form no cycle. The check is a depth-first search with the path in the error.
  • When participants is set, every flow's from and to and every included fragment's participants are in it.
  • FlowSecurity.SignedBy, TokenDefinition.VerifiedBy and TokenClaim.CheckedBy reference entity IDs. Issues/Verifies reference token IDs.
  • ParallelBranch.FlowRefs inside a scenario are indices into that scenario's flows.

The existing per-flow checks in validate_flow.go run on each scenario's flows. Errors carry the path, for example scenarios[2].flows[4].to.

docs.title: 4. Projection (scenario.go)
docs.text:
type ProjectOptions struct {
    Expand bool // inline included fragments; default renders them as include steps
}

// Scenario returns a single-flow Protocol for scenario id. Entities are
// filtered to the scenario's participants in entity order; phases are
// filtered to those referenced, in phase order; metadata is copied.
func (p *Protocol) Scenario(id string, opts ProjectOptions) (*Protocol, error)

// Legacy files: Scenario("", opts) returns p unchanged when Scenarios is empty.
  • With Expand, include steps are replaced recursively by the fragment's flows. Index-based references are re-based onto the expanded list.
  • Without Expand, include steps stay in Flows. Renderers that do not understand includes would break, so each sequence renderer gains an include case (section 5), and non-sequence renderers (DOT, network, infographic) always receive an expanded projection.
  • The projected protocol carries the scenario's id and name in ProtocolMeta (Name: "<protocol> — <scenario>") so titles render without renderer changes.

Executor and debugger run on a projection with Expand: true. Their index-based code is unchanged.

docs.title: 5. Rendering includes (collapsed)
docs.text:
The box spans the fragment's participants, from the first to the last in entity order.

Format Output PlantUML ref over a, b : <fragment name> Mermaid rect rgb(...) block containing Note over a,b: <fragment name> D2 sequence a group labeled with the fragment name, spanning the participants SVG a rounded rectangle across the participant lifelines, labeled

Golden files in render/testdata cover each format.

docs.title: 6. CLI (cmd/pidl)
docs.text:
• generate, simulate, debug and analyze take --scenario <id>. On a file with scenarios, omitting it is an error that lists the available IDs in order, except for analyze, which runs on all.
  • generate --all-scenarios -o <dir> writes NN-<scenario-id>.<ext>. NN is the 1-based position among non-fragment scenarios, zero-padded to at least two digits (wider when there are 100 or more scenarios). --include-fragments adds fragments after the main scenarios, with continued numbering.
  • --expand on generate inlines fragments.
  • New formats on generate:
  • scenario-matrix (Markdown) — rows are entities in order, columns are scenarios in order, cells mark participation.
  • token-table (Markdown) — rows are tokens in array order, with issuer, audience, binding, verified by and claims.
  • outline (Markdown) and outline-json — protocol, then roles in order with descriptions, then scenarios in order with each step's label (includes shown by fragment name). This is the input for deck and guide tooling.
  • pidl scenarios <file> lists scenarios in order, with the participant count, flow count and fragment flag. -f json gives JSON output.

docs.title: 7. Analyzer (analyze)
docs.text:
New rules, each with an ID, a severity and an explanation:

Rule Reports SEC017 Unused role an entity that no flow uses SEC018 Token checked before issued a flow verifies a token that no earlier step of the expanded scenario issues; tokens no flow issues are treated as external and skipped SEC019 Signer differs from sender or token holder signed_by differs from from, or a request presents a token that an earlier step delivered to someone other than the signer (the AAuth four-party agent_jkt case); skipped when the flow has a security annotation SEC020 Token verifier mismatch a flow's receiver checks a token whose verified_by does not list it SEC021 Unused fragment a fragment no scenario includes

Rules carry a scope. Flow rules (the existing SEC001 to SEC016) check Protocol.Flatten() for a document with scenarios; document rules receive the protocol as written and report scenario paths such as scenarios[1].flows[0] (exchange).

docs.title: 8. Composition (resolve.go)
docs.text:
• mergeBase: base scenarios come first. A derived scenario with the same id replaces the base one in its base position, so an override never reorders scenarios. New derived scenarios follow.
  • ExcludeScenarios runs before the merge. ExcludeEntities also drops scenario flows that reference an excluded entity and removes it from participants. ExcludePhases also clears phase references in scenario flows.
  • mergeImport: ProtocolImport.Scenarios []string selects scenarios to import. Fragments they include come with them, in the imported document's order. The alias prefix applies to scenario IDs, include targets, entity references, participants and phases.
  • Mixing documents with and without scenarios: when composition leaves both top-level flows and scenarios, the flows become the first scenario, with the resolved protocol's ID and name (plus a -flows suffix if that ID is taken).
  • The JSON Schema does not yet describe extends or imports; that gap predates this initiative.

docs.title: 9. Diff (compare.go)
docs.text:
• Scenarios are matched by id. The diff reports added, removed and renamed scenarios (same id, new name), as well as changed flows within each matched scenario, using the existing flow diff.
  • Order changes are reported separately for entities and scenarios ("moved from position 3 to 1").

docs.title: 10. Schema and specification
docs.text:
• schema/pidl.schema.json:
  • The top-level required drops flows.
  • It gains a oneOf requiring either a non-empty flows or a non-empty scenarios.
  • It gains the scenario and tokenClaim definitions, plus the new fields on flow, flowSecurity, tokenDefinition and extends.
  • docs/SPECIFICATION.md gets a "Scenarios" section and an "Ordering" section with the rules from section 2.

docs.title: Sequencing Constraints
docs.text:
• Types and validation come before projection, and projection before any renderer or CLI change.
  • Rendering includes depends on projection without expansion.
  • The analyzer rules depend on the verification fields.
  • The AAuth example depends on includes, verification fields and rendering. It serves as the end-to-end test.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Byte-for-byte compatibility. Changing a renderer for includes could alter output for legacy files. Mitigation: the existing golden files must pass unchanged, and include rendering only runs when a flow has Include set.
  • Unused-participant declarations. Projection drops entities a scenario does not use. Legacy files are not projected, so their output is unchanged.
  • Index re-basing on expansion. Errors here would misreport validation paths. Mitigation: table tests covering nested includes with parallel branches.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• Unit tests:
  • ordering helpers
  • each validation rule, both pass and fail cases
  • projection with and without expansion, including nested fragments
  • cycle detection
  • Golden files: each sequence format for a collapsed include, an expanded include and the AAuth main scenarios.
  • CLI table tests: --scenario, --all-scenarios file naming and ordering, scenarios listing, and errors.
  • Determinism: render every format twice and compare the outputs. Also shuffle map-backed metadata by re-encoding the input and confirm the output is unchanged.
  • Schema: every file in examples/ validates against the updated schema.

docs.title: PRD — Protocol walkthrough viewer and AAuth examples
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-PIDL-002 Repository: github.com/grokify/pidl

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
PIDL v0.7.0 can describe a protocol's roles and scenarios and render each scenario as a static sequence diagram. Static diagrams are a poor way to learn a protocol like AAuth:

  1. No step-by-step view. A five-party diagram with a dozen messages shows everything at once. A presenter cannot walk an audience through it one message at a time, and a reader cannot tell which roles take part in a given step.
  2. No message content. A diagram shows that the agent sends a resource token to the PS, but not what that request looks like: the signature headers, the body, or the claims inside the token. Readers have to cross-reference the specification.
  3. No connection between steps. A protocol's security depends on values that link steps: a resource token's agent_jkt must match the key that signs the request; presented_jti must match the token the agent presented. Static diagrams cannot show those links.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• A generic viewer for any PIDL file: pick a scenario, step forward and backward through it, and see the active step highlighted on the sequence diagram (its two roles, its arrow and its label).
  • Example requests, responses and decoded tokens for each step, shown beside the diagram.
  • A 16:9 presentation layout that works full screen in a talk and in a browser tab.
  • One self-contained HTML file per protocol, with no server, so a walkthrough can be shared by sending a file.
  • A fully worked AAuth draft-11 example: every step of the five access modes and their fragments with requests, responses and tokens taken from or derived from the draft, using consistent values across steps.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Message schemas or protocol conformance checking. Examples are illustrative.
  • Editing PIDL in the viewer.
  • Live protocol execution against real servers.
  • Replacing the static diagram formats; the viewer is an additional output.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
• Presenters explaining a protocol in a talk or meeting.
  • Readers learning a protocol from its PIDL description.
  • Spec reviewers checking that the values each step relies on line up end to end.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
1. Flow examples. A flow MAY carry an example with a source (citation), a kind (draft: taken from the source with values aligned; derived: written from the source's normative text), an HTTP request and/or response (method or status, URL, ordered headers, body), and decoded tokens (header and payload) keyed to token definitions.
  2. Validation. kind is draft or derived; source is required; header names are non-empty; token references resolve to token definitions.
  3. Walkthrough model. The library produces a walkthrough document: protocol, roles in entities order, and for each scenario in output order its fully expanded steps. Each step carries its position, from and to roles, label, response flag, the fragments it sits inside, note, example, and analyzer findings located at that flow.
  4. Walkthrough output. generate -f walkthrough-json writes the walkthrough model.
  5. Viewer layout. A top bar with the protocol name and a scenario selector; a sequence diagram on the left; the request on the upper right; the response on the lower right; step controls.
  6. Stepping. Next and previous buttons, arrow keys, and Home/End. The active step's arrow, label and two role headers are highlighted; earlier steps are dimmed; later steps are faint. The URL hash records the scenario and step.
  7. Fragments. Steps inside an included fragment show the fragment's name; the diagram groups them visually.
  8. Tokens. Decoded token header and payload are shown in readable form; claims a step's receiver checks are highlighted.
  9. Findings and notes. A step's notes and analyzer findings appear as callouts.
  10. Example provenance. Each example shows its source and a draft or derived badge.
  11. Single-file output. generate -f viewer writes one HTML file containing the viewer and the walkthrough data.
  12. AAuth examples. The aauth_protocol example gains examples for every HTTP step of all five scenarios and three fragments, with one consistent set of identifiers, keys and token values.

docs.title: Non-Functional
docs.text:
• The viewer renders the AAuth walkthrough in under a second on a laptop and works offline.
  • The viewer's built HTML is reproducible from source with one documented command.
  • Go code remains library-first; the viewer contains presentation logic only.
  • Existing output formats are unchanged.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• pidl generate -f viewer aauth_protocol -o aauth.html produces a file that opens in a browser and steps through all five AAuth scenarios.
  • In the federated scenario, stepping to the PS-to-AS request shows the request signed with the PS's key and the resource token whose agent_jkt names the agent's key, with the SEC019 finding as a callout.
  • Every AAuth example cites a draft-11 section.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Examples live in the PIDL file as an optional per-flow field, so they travel with the protocol.
  • Provenance is explicit. draft examples come from the draft with values aligned to the scenario; derived examples are written from normative text. The viewer shows which.
  • Go computes, the viewer renders. Include expansion, ordering and findings come from the Go library through the walkthrough model, so the viewer does not reimplement PIDL semantics.
  • Self-contained HTML. The viewer is built into a single file and embedded in the Go binary.
  • Ships as v0.8.0.

docs.title: 1. Flow examples (types.go)

type FlowExample struct {
    Source   string            `json:"source"`             // e.g. "draft-11 §7.2.1"
    Kind     ExampleKind       `json:"kind"`               // "draft" | "derived"
    Request  *ExampleRequest   `json:"request,omitempty"`
    Response *ExampleResponse  `json:"response,omitempty"`
    Tokens   []ExampleToken    `json:"tokens,omitempty"`
    Note     string            `json:"note,omitempty"`
}
type ExampleRequest struct {
    Method  string          `json:"method"`
    URL     string          `json:"url"`
    Headers []ExampleHeader `json:"headers,omitempty"`
    Body    json.RawMessage `json:"body,omitempty"`
}
type ExampleResponse struct {
    Status  int             `json:"status"`
    Headers []ExampleHeader `json:"headers,omitempty"`
    Body    json.RawMessage `json:"body,omitempty"`
}
type ExampleHeader struct {
    Name  string `json:"name"`
    Value string `json:"value"`
}
type ExampleToken struct {

    Label   string          `json:"label,omitempty"`   // e.g. "in Signature-Key"

}
// Flow gains: Example *FlowExample `json:"example,omitempty"`

docs.title: 2. Walkthrough model (walkthrough.go)

    Roles     []OutlineRole

}

    Participants []string
    Steps []WalkthroughStep
}
type WalkthroughStep struct {
    Number   int      // 1-based within the expanded scenario
    From, To string
    Label    string
    Response bool
    Phase    string
    Fragments []string   // fragment names, outermost first
    Note     string
    Example  *FlowExample
    Location string      // written location, e.g. "scenarios[1].flows[0] (consent)"
    Findings []WalkthroughFinding
}
type WalkthroughFinding struct { ID, Severity, Title, Description string }

func (p *Protocol) Walkthrough(findings func(*Protocol) []Finding) Walkthrough
  • Steps come from expanding includes in order, recording each enclosing fragment's name.
  • Location uses the same strings as the analyzer's document rules, so findings attach by location. The pidl package cannot import analyze, so the caller passes findings in; the CLI and renderer run the analyzer.
  • Include steps disappear in expansion; their fragment name appears in Fragments of the inlined steps.

docs.title: 3. Formats
docs.text:
• walkthrough-json: the walkthrough model as JSON, a whole-file format.
  • viewer: the built viewer HTML with the walkthrough JSON embedded in a <script type="application/json" id="pidl-walkthrough"> element, a whole-file format.

docs.title: 4. Viewer app (viewer/)
docs.text:
• Vite 8, React 19, TypeScript, vite-plugin-singlefile; Vitest for unit tests.
  • Data: reads the embedded #pidl-walkthrough element; in development, loads public/walkthrough.json.
  • Layout: a fixed 1600×900 stage scaled to fit the window (16:9). Top bar: protocol name, scenario selector, step counter and controls. Left (60%): SVG sequence diagram drawn by the app. Right (40%): request panel above, response panel below, each with tabs for HTTP and tokens.
  • Diagram: role headers in walkthrough role order, limited to the scenario's participants; one row per step; fragment groups drawn as shaded bands labeled with the fragment name; the active step's arrow, label and role headers highlighted, earlier steps dimmed, later steps faint. The diagram scrolls to keep the active step visible.
  • Stepping: buttons, Left/Right arrows, Home/End; URL hash #<scenario-id>/<step>.
  • Panels: method, URL and headers; JSON body pretty-printed; decoded tokens with claims named in the receiver's checked_by highlighted; provenance badge (draft or derived) with source; notes and findings as callouts.
  • Theme: light and dark via prefers-color-scheme.

docs.title: 5. Build and embedding
docs.text:
• npm run build in viewer/ writes render/viewer/viewer.html (committed), which render embeds with go:embed.
  • go generate ./render/... runs the build; CI checks that the committed file matches a fresh build.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Committed build artifact drift. Mitigation: a CI check rebuilds and diffs.
  • Example accuracy. Examples could misstate the draft. Mitigation: each cites a section; draft versus derived is explicit; consistent identifiers are listed once in the example file's description of values.
  • Large diagrams. Five-party scenarios with fifteen steps must stay legible at 16:9. Mitigation: the diagram scrolls and keeps the active step in view.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• Go: validation table tests for examples; walkthrough expansion with nested fragments, locations and findings; golden files for walkthrough-json; viewer output contains the embedded data.
  • Viewer: Vitest unit tests for layout computation, step navigation and hash parsing.
  • Manual: open the AAuth viewer in a browser and step through every scenario; screenshots in the PR.
